title: OEIS anchor: U(n) = A192787
connection: Our unordered count U(n) of 4/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z (x≤y≤z) reproduces A192787 term-for-term (n ≤ 30 000 computed); the entry's links/comments are the natural index of prior counting work.
why: Validates the counting engine and gives a curated reference list (Vaughan, Elsholtz–Tao, Swett) for every other fingerprint.
first_step: Read the A192787 entry's references/links and cross-references; record any formula or conjecture not already in FRONTIER.md.

title: OEIS anchor: distinct-solution count D(n) = A073101
connection: D(n) (x<y<z) matches A073101; D(n)=0 only at n=2 for n ≤ 30 000, i.e. ES with distinct denominators holds 3..30 000.
why: Distinctness is the standard Egyptian-fraction convention; A073101 cross-refs may list distinct-only variants with known exceptions.
first_step: Read A073101 cross-references for 'distinct' and 'k-term' variants; check whether any proved bound for D(n) is better than for U(n).

title: OEIS anchor: ordered count O(n) = A292581, at primes A292624
connection: O(n) (ordered triples) matches A292581, and O(p) matches A292624; U(p) matches A192789.
why: Three independent OEIS entries anchor the prime-restricted counts used in all correlation items below.
first_step: Pull b-files of A292624/A192789 to extend our prime data past 2·10⁵ for free, if they go further.

title: OEIS anchor: min max-denominator = A337432
connection: Our minz(n) (least possible largest denominator) matches A337432; it is the 'smallest-z' ES fingerprint.
why: A small minimal z is a constructive certificate; the entry may contain a conjectured growth bound useful as a heuristic target.
first_step: Read A337432 comments for a conjectured bound minz(n) ≪ n^{1+ε} or similar; compare to our records 2,3,10,14,33,52,102,138,232,…

title: OEIS anchors for 5/n and 6/n: A226644, A226645
why: The m-family is the Sierpiński/Schinzel generalisation; missing entries for m ≥ 7 are a gap a curator could fill and a sign the m-family data is unexplored.
first_step: Submit U_m(n) for m = 7..13 to OEIS (data in data/z52b/raw/m*_4000.txt) after checking against a second implementation.

title: O(n) is odd ⟺ n ≡ 2 (mod 4) for 2 ≤ n ≤ 30 000 (S₃-orbit parity)
connection: Ordered count = #(x=y=z) + 3·#(exactly two equal) + 6·#(distinct), so O(n) ≡ #(all equal) + #(two equal) (mod 2); in range this is odd exactly for n ≡ 2 (mod 4) (the OEIS hit A121262 for 'O mod 2' was an offset artefact of starting at n = 2). Also O(n) ≢ 0 (mod 6) ⟺ n even (in range).
why: Parity of a count via its degenerate (isosceles/equilateral) solutions is the 'involution' template of WINDMILL.md; here the degenerate solutions are fully classified by the isosceles factorisation (see the isosceles-law item), so the parity law should be provable.
first_step: Prove the n ≡ 2 (mod 4) law by counting isosceles solutions via (4x−2n)(4z−n) = 2n² and (4x−n)(4z−2n) = 2n² and the equilateral one (3n/4 integral); then look for a finer involution on U(p) at p ≡ 1 (4) (where there are no degenerate solutions).

title: U(n) never equals 5 (n ≤ 30 000)
connection: The value 5 is the only k ≤ 500 not attained by U(n) for 2 ≤ n ≤ 30 000; at primes ≤ 2·10⁵ the values 5 and 12 are never attained.
why: A gap in the value set is a cheap arithmetic fingerprint; if U(n) ≥ 6 eventually were provable by a structural lower bound it would be a (weak) quantitative ES statement for large n — but likely just small-n accident.
first_step: Extend U(n) to n ≤ 10⁵ and check whether U(n) = 5 ever appears; list all n with U(n) ≤ 8 and test whether they are all ≤ some bound.

title: U(p) ≤ 4 only for p ∈ {2,3,5,13,17}
connection: Among primes ≤ 2·10⁵, U(p) ≤ 4 only at 2,3,5,13,17; for p > 1000 min U(p) is 9 (at 2521), 11, 15, …
why: An explicit lower bound U(p) ≥ c log²p failing only at small p is the kind of statement the BM main-term work (FRONTIER §2.2) predicts; the empirical floor calibrates c.
first_step: Fit min_{p∈[X,2X]} U(p) vs (log X)² for X up to 10⁷ (count program runs in ~1 s per prime at 10⁶).

title: Least prime with U(p) = 6 is 193 (a Type-A failure)
connection: The sequence 'least prime p with U(p)=k' begins 2,5,3,13,–,193,7,97,11,89,19,–,53,…; 193 (López Type-A failure) is the first prime with exactly six solutions.
why: Hard primes for one certificate family show up as the first occurrences of small U-values, i.e. the count sees the same arithmetic.
first_step: Tabulate, for each k ≤ 40, the least p with U(p)=k and check whether these are enriched in p ≡ 1 (24) and in the m/p-failure sets (data/z52b/raw/m*_pr1e5.txt).

title: Record lows of U(p)/log²p are 53, 61, 73, 193, 2521
connection: Scanning primes 50 < p < 2·10⁵, U(p)/log²p sets record lows exactly at 53, 61, 73, 193, 2521 (ratio 0.147 at 2521); no further record up to 2·10⁵.
why: Two of the five records are the Type-A (b=1) failures 193, 2521; the record sequence is a compact 'hardness' fingerprint not in OEIS.
first_step: Extend to 10⁷ with the count program restricted to candidates p ≡ 1 (mod 840) or with large least-QNR (cheap pre-filter), to see if 66529 or other A/R failures become records.

title: 2521 = lcm(1..9) + 1 is the hardest prime ≤ 2·10⁵
connection: 2521 = lcm(1,…,10)+1 minimises U(p)/log²p over primes ≤ 2·10⁵ (U=9); the primes lcm(1..k)+1 = 7, 13, 61, 421, 2521 have ratios 1.85, 0.61, 0.65, 0.44, 0.15 — monotone towards hard.
why: p ≡ 1 mod every small prime power makes every small prime a QR mod p and kills all small-modulus covering identities simultaneously; this is the extremal configuration for Mordell-type coverings.
first_step: Compute U, R, Uv for the next such prime 232 792 561 = lcm(1..19)+1 (≈ 1–2 h with the count program; words sieve to 2.4·10⁸ is cheaper) and test whether it is a (★) or b=1 failure.

title: Prediction: 232 792 561 should be an extreme ES-hard prime
connection: By the lcm(1..k)+1 heuristic, p = 232 792 561 (prime, = lcm(1..19)+1) has all primes ≤ 19 as QRs and p ≡ 1 mod 2⁴·3²·5·7·11·13·17·19; expect U(p)/log²p far below every prime of comparable size.
why: A falsifiable fingerprint: if confirmed it shows hardness is governed by the multiplicative structure of p−1 (smoothness) and quadratic character at small primes — the exact data a covering/sieve argument must beat.
first_step: Run z52b_count on 232792561 (needs ~3 GB spf sieve; or patch to factor x by trial division) and check R(p) via the words sieve extended to 2.4·10⁸.

title: ES-hard primes vs pseudosquares (A002189)
connection: Least primes p≡1(4) with least QNR = 2,3,5,…,47: 5,17,73,241,1009,2689,8089,33049,53881,87481,483289,515761,1083289,7921489,3818929; the first terms match OEIS A102295 (record least-QNR primes); several (73, 241, 53881, 87481) coincide with Lehmer pseudosquares A002189 and with our 40 hardest primes.
why: Quadratic-residue covering is exactly what pseudosquares defeat (Lehmer–Lehmer–Shanks sieve); ES Type I/II identities are QR conditions, so pseudosquare theory (Schinzel's GRH bounds on pseudosquare growth) may bound how long all small identities can fail.
first_step: Compute U(p)/log²p for the pseudosquare primes up to 10⁸ and compare to random p≡1(840) of the same size; read Lukes–Patterson–Williams on pseudosquares and Schinzel's 1997 bound.

title: U(p) at least-QNR-record primes is only moderately small
connection: At the least p≡1(4) with least QNR q (q=11..47), U(p)/log²p = 0.40,0.37,0.54,0.53,0.36,0.29,0.60,0.53,0.55,0.67,0.61 — below typical (≈1–2) but not record-hard; 2521 (least QNR 11) is far harder (0.15).
why: Shows hardness is not a function of the least QNR alone: p−1 smoothness / p ≡ 1 mod higher prime powers adds a second axis — useful for designing a two-parameter hardness model.
first_step: Regress log U(p) on log L(1,χ_p) and log(σ(p−1)/(p−1)) jointly; check which explains 2521 vs 87481.

title: U(p) residual is driven by L(1,χ_p) (Spearman −0.69)
connection: At ≈9 000 primes p≡1(4) <2·10⁵, the residual of log U(p) (after log p, loglog p) has Spearman ρ = −0.69 with L(1,χ_p) = 2h(p)·log ε_p/√p (real quadratic field Q(√p)); more small QRs ⇒ fewer solutions.
why: Gives a concrete arithmetic 'explanatory variable' for the ES count; the BM main term T(p) = Σ (−uB/p)/φ(4uB) (FRONTIER §2.2) is a weighted sum of the same character, so this is the data face of BM.
first_step: Prove/derive the expected-count heuristic E U(p) ≈ c(log p)² · F(χ_p) with F a finite Euler product, and compare F with our fitted exponent (−0.30).

title: log U(p) ≈ const − 0.30·log L_Q(1,χ_p), saturating at Q ≈ 30
connection: Adding log of the truncated Euler product ∏_{q≤Q}(1−χ_p(q)/q)^{−1} to the (log p, loglog p) regression gives α ≈ −0.30 and R²-gain 0.29 (Q=2), 0.40 (Q=3), 0.47 (Q=7), 0.49 (Q=31), 0.48 (Q=1000).
why: About half the residual variance of log U(p) is explained by the quadratic character of p at primes ≤ 30; this suggests (it does not prove) that much of the count's fluctuation is governed by finitely many local data.
first_step: Fit with separate coefficients per small prime q (2,3,5,7,11,13) to get the local weights; compare to the Elsholtz–Tao local densities.

title: Type II count k₂(p) prefers L(1,χ_{−4p}) large (α ≈ +0.21)
connection: Solutions with two denominators divisible by p (k₂) correlate positively with L(1,χ_{−4p}) = πh(−4p)/(2√p) (ρ=+0.37) and negatively with L(1,χ_p) (α ≈ −0.20); Type I (k₁) sees only χ_p (α ≈ −0.34, χ_{−4p} gain ≈ 0).
why: The two ET types live on different quadratic twists (χ_p vs χ_{−4p} = χ_{−1}χ_p at odd q): a natural 'complementarity' — when one type is starved by its character, the other may be fed.
first_step: Test the complementarity: correlation between k₁ and k₂ residuals; is min(k₁,k₂) ever 0 at p ≡ 1 (4) and if so, is the other large?

title: (★) count R(p) correlates with h(−4p) (α ≈ +0.38, R²-gain 0.20)
connection: The c=1 Type-II line R(p) = #{4uBC−u−B=p} fits log R ≈ … + 0.38 log L_Q(1,χ_{−4p}) (gain 0.20) and only −0.17 on χ_p (gain 0.09).
why: R(p) is the campaign's central count; a class-number dependence suggests an exact or approximate formula in terms of h(−4p)/Hurwitz numbers (theta-series origin), cf. KUDLA_ES.md.
first_step: Fit log R(p) on log L(1,χ_{dp}) for twists d ∈ {−4,−8,−3,−20,…} jointly (class numbers themselves scale like √p, R like log²p, so only L-values/Euler products can enter); identify the minimal twist set.

title: U(p) uncorrelated with a_p of non-CM elliptic curves
connection: Spearman of U(p)-residual with a_p(11a1)/2√p is +0.004, with a_p(37a1)/2√p −0.005, with |a_p(32a1)|/2√p +0.007, with Ramanujan τ(p)/p^{5.5} +0.006 (n≈9 000).
why: Null result: no detectable dependence on these Hecke eigenvalues, so a naive 'ES count tracks a fixed non-CM form' fingerprint is not supported; the detected dependence is through quadratic characters/L-values.
first_step: Repeat with weight-2 newforms of level 4·d for d | 840 and with weight-3/2 forms (Shimura lifts) where class numbers do appear.

title: a_p(32a1) mod 8 is just (2/p)
connection: The strong correlation of U(p) with a_p(y²=x³−x) mod 8 (ρ=+0.55) is identical to that with (2/p) (ρ=−0.55): for this CM curve a_p mod 8 encodes p mod 8.
why: Records a spurious-looking modular-form 'match' and its trivial explanation (guard against false fingerprints).
first_step: None needed; use as a sanity check whenever a CM form correlates.

title: (7/p) anomaly: U(p) does not see the character at 7
connection: Residual Spearman of U(p) with (2/p), (3/p), (5/p) is −0.55, −0.31, −0.28 but with (7/p) only −0.013, although Mordell's classes p ≡ 3,5,6 (mod 7) are covered by identities.
why: Suggests the mod-7 identity contributes O(1) solutions while 2,3,5 contribute families ∝ log p; identifies which local primes matter for the count — relevant to any weighted covering.
first_step: Split U(p) by p mod 7 class and by whether the mod-7 identity solution exists; check whether the 7-family has bounded size.

title: U(p) vs least QNR: ρ = −0.66
connection: Residual of U(p) correlates −0.66 with the least quadratic non-residue of p and +0.46 with #QNR among primes ≤ 29.
why: Least-QNR is Burgess/Vinogradov territory; a proof that U(p) ≥ 1 using 'some small prime is a QNR' (Linnik–Vinogradov n₂(p) ≪ p^{1/(4√e)+ε}) is exactly the Type-I mechanism.
first_step: Write the Type-I count as a sum over QNRs and check numerically that its main term scales with #QNR ≤ log p.

title: U(p) vs least primitive root: ρ = −0.57
connection: Residual U(p) correlates −0.57 with the least primitive root g(p), and +0.45 with ord_p(2)/(p−1).
why: Probably a proxy for the least QNR (a primitive root is a QNR), but ord_p(2) carries more than (2/p): worth separating.
first_step: Partial correlation of U with ord_p(2)/(p−1) controlling for (2/p) and least QNR.

title: U(p) vs τ(p−1) and σ(p−1)/(p−1): ρ ≈ −0.53
connection: More divisors of p−1 ⇒ fewer ES solutions (ρ(τ(p−1)) = −0.53, ρ(σ(p−1)/(p−1)) = −0.53, ρ(φ(p−1)/(p−1)) = +0.42).
why: Smooth p−1 means p ≡ 1 modulo many small numbers — the Mordell-class obstruction; links ES hardness to the Erdős–Pomerance world of smooth shifted primes.
first_step: Test whether τ(p−1) remains significant after controlling for L(1,χ_p) (partial correlation).

title: U(p) vs τ((p+3)/4): ρ = +0.59
connection: U(p) residual correlates +0.59 with τ((p+3)/4) and +0.48 with τ(p+3), but only +0.12 with τ(4p+1), +0.12 with τ(p+4), +0.05 with τ(p+12).
why: x = (p+3)/4 is the smallest admissible first denominator; solutions with x=(p+3)/4 come from divisors of (p+3)/4-related numbers; a single shift explains a large share of variance.
first_step: Count solutions by x−⌈p/4⌉ ∈ {0,1,2,…} and measure what fraction of U(p) comes from the first few x; relate to divisors of p+3, p+7, …

title: Real quadratic regulator log ε_p anticorrelates with U(p) (ρ = −0.44)
connection: log ε_p and log ε_p/√p correlate −0.44 / −0.51 with U(p)-residual; h(p) alone ≈ 0 (−0.04); CF period of √p −0.27.
why: By the class number formula, 2h(p)R/√p = L(1,χ_p) (R = log ε_p): the regulator carries the L-value since h(p)=1 mostly; a direct ES ↔ fundamental unit link is the CF/Pell side of the CF-length forms of ES (ES₅).
first_step: Correlate the five-slice / λ(p) ≤ 3 certificate counts with the CF period of √p and with the regulator.

title: h(−3p) correlates positively with U(p) (ρ=+0.46)
connection: U(p) residual vs h(−3p) (imaginary quadratic field Q(√−3p)) ρ = +0.46; vs h(−4p) only +0.08 (raw) / +0.14 (normalised).
why: χ_{−3p}(q) = (−3/q)(p/q): another twist; ES identities with denominator 3 (p ≡ 2 mod 3 classes) suggest the −3 twist is natural.
first_step: Fit log U on all of log L(1,χ_{dp}) for d ∈ {1,−1,−3,−4,−8,5,−20,…} jointly and identify the minimal set.

title: Uv(p) (U-certificates) ~ U(p): ρ = +0.64; R(p) only +0.24
connection: The ES count U(p) correlates +0.64 with the U-certificate word count Uv(p), +0.46 with I3(p), +0.32 with W(p) but only +0.24 with the (★) count R(p).
why: R(p) is a thin slice with its own character (χ_{−4p}); Uv tracks the whole count. Useful when choosing which certificate family to attack for a lower bound proportional to U(p).
first_step: Compute what fraction of each p's ES solutions correspond to (★), U, I3 words via the explicit maps; check whether the fraction is stable.

title: minz(p) is always a multiple of p (p ≤ 2·10⁵)
connection: For every prime p ≤ 2·10⁵ the least possible largest denominator minz(p) ≡ 0 (mod p) (OEIS-style constant-zero transform).
why: If provable it pins the optimal solution's structure: the largest denominator always carries p; could give an extremal-solution parametrisation and a minimal-height bound.
first_step: Try to prove: in any solution of 4/p with largest denominator z, if p ∤ z then z ≥ … > some solution with p | z; else find a counterexample for composite-free p beyond 2·10⁵.

title: minz(p)/p sequence: 1,1,2,2,3,4,6,3,6,8,8,10,… (not in OEIS)
connection: floor(minz(p)/p) at primes; at p≡1(4): 2,4,6,8,10,4,14,9,10,8,28,7,…; minz(p)/p correlates −0.42 with τ(4p+1) and −0.31 with R(p).
why: The cofactor of p in the optimal denominator is a 'height' of the cheapest certificate; small values relate to (★) with small C (divisors of 4Cp+1).
first_step: Identify minz(p)/p with the least C such that 4Cp+1 has a divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4C) or similar; test equality over our range.

title: Height growth: max_{p≤X} minz(p)/p
connection: Record values of minz(p) occur at 2,3,5,7,11,13,17,23,29,31,37,53,… (nearly every prime early on); record minz(p)/p would measure the worst certificate height.
why: An upper bound minz(p) ≤ p^{1+θ} for all p is equivalent to ES with a height bound; empirical θ guides which 'bounded C' statement to aim for.
first_step: Compute max_{p ≤ X} log(minz(p)/p)/log p for X up to 10⁷ and fit.

title: n ∤ minlcm(n) ⟺ 4 | n
connection: The least common denominator of a solution of 4/n is divisible by n except exactly when 4 | n (data n ≤ 30 000; OEIS A008586 match for the exception positions).
why: Trivial direction: 4|n gives 4/n = 1/(n/4)·… with smaller lcm; but the converse (n | lcm for 4 ∤ n) is a clean lemma ensuring p-adic content of every solution.
first_step: Prove: if 4 ∤ n then every solution's lcm is divisible by n (consider v_q of both sides for q^a ∥ n).

title: minlcm(p)/p at primes not in OEIS; correlates +0.23 with least QNR
connection: The least common denominator over solutions, divided by p, behaves like a cost: larger when small primes are QRs (ρ=+0.23 with least QNR, +0.20 with L(1,χ_p)).
why: Smallest common denominator = smallest N with 4N/p a sum of three divisors of N (Egyptian-fraction 'practical number' view) — links ES to practical numbers / Erdős–Graham denominators.
first_step: Check: is minlcm(p)/p always a practical number? Compute and compare to OEIS A005153.

title: Mordell classes: x = (n+3)/4 fails only for n ≡ 1 (mod 24)
why: The sequence (not in OEIS) is the failure set of the single simplest identity family; its intersection with R-zeros and Type-A failures shows which hard primes the 'greedy' family catches.
first_step: Characterise: n with no solution with x=(n+3)/4 ⟺ 12/(n(n+3)) not a sum of two unit fractions ⟺ no divisor pair condition; derive the density and compare to count 373 ≤ 30 000.

title: Greedy-failure composites: 49, 169, 361, 553, … (squares and products)
connection: The composite members of the x=(n+3)/4 failure set include many odd squares ≡ 1 (24) (49, 169, 361, 961, 1369, …) but not all (25 is certified: 4/25 = 1/7 + 1/70 + 1/350 with 7 = (25+3)/4), and non-squares like 553 = 7·79, 721, 793, 889.
why: Squares are over-represented (a T1-like effect for a single identity family) but not uniformly obstructed; non-square composite failures show the obstruction is not only quadratic.
first_step: List non-square composite members ≤ 10⁵ and check whether each factors into primes that are themselves failures (multiplicativity test).

title: U(n) records at 2,3,6,8,10,12,15,24,30,40,48,60,… vs highly composite numbers
connection: Record positions of U(n) (not in OEIS) are dominated by smooth numbers but are not A002182 (15, 30, 40 appear; 36 does not).
why: Records of a divisor-sum-like count should track the extremal order of a specific divisor function; identifying it gives the right 'max U(n) ≍ ?' growth.
first_step: Compare record positions with records of Σ_{d|n} τ(d)², τ(n)τ(n+1)…; fit max_{n≤X} U(n) vs exp(c log X/log log X).

title: Record U(p) at primes: 2,3,7,11,19,23,47,71,167,191,239,359,…
connection: Primes setting U(p) records are all ≡ 3 (mod 4) beyond 2,3 and mostly ≡ 23 (mod 24) (p+1 highly divisible); identical record set for O(p).
why: Mirror image of hard primes: maximal counts at p ≡ −1 modulo many small numbers — ES 'easy' primes are near-smooth p+1.
first_step: Check if record primes satisfy p+1 = smooth with record τ(p+1); OEIS search of the record list (no match).

title: U(p) mod m is equidistributed (small bias at U ≡ 1 mod 6)
connection: For p≡1(4) >100 (n=8 843), U(p) mod 2,3,4,8 are flat within noise; U(p) ≡ 1 (mod 6) is 1361 vs ≈1490 expected (≈3.5σ low).
why: No parity constraint ⇒ no simple involution explains U(p); the mod-6 dip may be a counting artefact (e.g. solutions with y=z).
first_step: Separate solutions with repeated denominators (x=y or y=z) and recount mod 6.

title: k₁(n), k₂(n) are new sequences
connection: Number of solutions of 4/n with exactly one (k₁) / two (k₂) denominators divisible by n: k₁ = 0,2,0,1,5,5,0,5,6,6,9,…; k₂ = 1,1,1,1,2,2,2,1,4,3,…; neither in OEIS.
why: At primes these are ET Type I/Type II counts; separate sequences make it possible for others to find formulas.
first_step: Submit both (with k₃ ≡ 0 for n>1, a trivial lemma) to OEIS after independent verification.

title: k₂(p) ≥ 1 for every prime p ≤ 2·10⁵
connection: Every prime ≤ 2·10⁵ has a solution with exactly two denominators divisible by p (Type II); min k₂(p) over p ≡ 1 (4) > 1000 is small but nonzero.
why: ET note Type II is the 'easier to count' type; empirical universality of Type II alone is the statement many campaign lines target.
first_step: Record the minimum k₂(p) per dyadic range and list primes with k₂(p) = 1.

title: k₁(p) can be small while k₂(p) is not — or vice versa?
connection: k₁ and k₂ have residual correlation driven by different characters; tabulating the joint distribution of (k₁(p), k₂(p)) shows whether simultaneous smallness is rarer than independence predicts.
why: Anti-correlation of the types' local obstructions would be the cleanest heuristic for 'one type always works'.
first_step: Compute Spearman(k₁ residual, k₂ residual) and the count of p with both below their 5% quantiles vs 0.25% expected.

title: nx(n): number of distinct first denominators
connection: nx(n) = #{x : some solution has this smallest denominator}: 1,2,2,1,3,3,4,3,4,3,6,2,… (not in OEIS); at primes correlates like U (ρ=−0.65 with L(1,χ_p)).
why: nx is the 'first-step branching' of the greedy tree; lower bounds on nx(p) are ES; it is the quantity a sieve over x controls.
first_step: Fit nx(p) vs log p (likely ≍ log p, not log²p) and check whether nx(p) ≥ 1 has a shorter proof form (one-shift divisibility).

title: maxx(p) − p/4 (largest smallest-denominator)
connection: The largest possible smallest denominator maxx(p) has maxx − p/4 weakly tied to least QNR (ρ=−0.19); maxx(p) ≤ 3p/4 always; the sequence is not in OEIS.
why: Measures how 'balanced' the most balanced solution can be (BALANCED_LATTICE.md); balanced solutions are rare and relate to the cubic surface's real-point distribution.
first_step: Plot (maxx(p) − p/4)/p; compare with the balanced-solution census in BALANCED_LATTICE.md.

title: U(p) at p ≡ 1 (24) vs p ≡ 1 (840) distributions
connection: Spearman of residual U(p) with 1[p≡1 mod 24] is −0.62, with '840-square class' −0.38, with 1[p≡1 mod 840] −0.15 (rare event).
why: Quantifies how much of hardness is the classical Mordell residue structure — a reference point for any proof that treats 'bad residue classes' separately.
first_step: Compute mean U(p)/log²p per class mod 840 (the six square classes 1,121,169,289,361,529) and rank them.

title: Which square class mod 840 is hardest?
connection: The six Mordell hard classes {1,121,169,289,361,529} mod 840 likely differ in mean U(p)/log²p; the 30 hardest primes ≤ 2·10⁵ fall in classes 1 (×9), 361 (×8), 121 (×6), 169 (×3), 289, 529 — and three outside the square classes (193, 241 ≡ 193, 241; 3169 ≡ 649).
why: Class-by-class constants feed directly into the BM main term per residue class and into covering-congruence choices.
first_step: Group primes ≤ 2·10⁵ by class mod 840 and by class mod 9240 = 840·11, compute mean and min of U(p)/log²p.

title: U(p) vs smoothness of p−1: ρ(P⁺(p−1) exponent) = +0.40
connection: log P⁺(p−1)/log p correlates +0.40 with U(p) residual: smooth p−1 ⇒ hard.
why: Smooth shifted primes have positive density for P⁺(p−1) ≤ p^{0.2961} (Baker–Harman, cited in FORCED_WINDOW.md); ES-hard primes may be concentrated there, which is a thin set amenable to separate treatment.
first_step: Estimate density of 'ES-hard' (ratio below 0.3) among primes with P⁺(p−1) ≤ p^{1/3} vs others.

title: Hard primes are p ≡ 1 mod a large smooth modulus — compare with Carmichael/Korselt primes
connection: 2521, 1201, 3361, 20521, 21841, 4201, 14401, 9601 all have p−1 divisible by 2⁴·3·5² or 2⁴·3·5·7 etc.; these are exactly the primes used to build Carmichael numbers (Erdős construction, p−1 | L).
why: Shared extremal structure (p−1 | L for smooth L) — tools for counting such primes (AGP, Erdős) could count ES-hard candidates.
first_step: Test: are ES-hard primes over-represented among prime factors of Carmichael numbers ≤ 10¹²? (Pinch's tables).

title: Hardest 30 primes ≤ 2·10⁵ by U/log² are all ≡ 1 (mod 24)
why: Confirms Mordell's classical reduction quantitatively and shows the hard set inside 1 (mod 24) is further structured by mod-5/7/9/16 conditions.
first_step: Compute the hard list's distribution mod 5, 7, 9, 16, 25 vs all p ≡ 1 (24) to measure each prime power's contribution.

title: Campaign hard-prime lists are not in OEIS
why: No hidden classical identity (e.g. 'primes p with property X of p−1') explains them — or OEIS lacks it; submission would expose them to outside pattern-finders.
first_step: Submit the R-zero list with a definition and b-file to OEIS; also add I3 zeros (114 terms) and U failures.

title: 5/n and 6/n: no 3-term failure (primes ≤ 10⁵, all n ≤ 4000)
connection: U₅(p), U₆(p) ≥ 1 for all primes 3..10⁵ and all n ≤ 4000 (6/n trivially follows from 3/n except tiny n).
why: Sierpiński's 5/n is the nearest sibling of ES; joint fingerprints (U₄(p), U₅(p)) can show whether the same primes are hard for both.
first_step: Compute Spearman(U₄(p)/log²p, U₅(p)/log²p) at p ≤ 10⁵ and list primes hard for both.
refs: arXiv:2511.16817 (Pomerance–Weingartner, Exceptions to the Erdős–Straus–Schinzel conjecture)

title: 7/n fails only at n = 2 (≤ 10⁵ primes, n ≤ 4000)
connection: Consistent with PW (no 7/n exception in [3, 10¹³]); 7/p counts at primes are small (U₇(p) = 0,1,2,3,2,8,4,…).
why: 7/n is the smallest numerator where the local (mod-m) obstruction picture differs from 4 and 5; any ES method that is numerator-uniform must also handle 7.
first_step: Fit U₇(p) vs log²p and check whether the hardest 7/p primes coincide with the hardest 4/p primes.
refs: arXiv:2511.16817 (Pomerance–Weingartner, Exceptions to the Erdős–Straus–Schinzel conjecture)

title: 'Even ES': every prime p > 241 has an ES solution with x, y, z all even (≤ 10⁵)
connection: 8/p = 1/x'+1/y'+1/z' ⟺ 4/p has a solution with 2 | x, y, z; failures at primes: {2,3,11,17,131,241} (known, PW Table 1).
why: A strictly stronger ES that holds beyond 241 numerically: proofs that produce even solutions (e.g. 2-adic/ parity-structured families) only need to beat finitely many exceptions.
first_step: Search for a polynomial/covering family giving all-even solutions for p ≡ 1 (24) and see which residue classes remain; compare with T1 at squares (do even squares-type obstructions exist?).
refs: arXiv:2511.16817 (Pomerance–Weingartner, Exceptions to the Erdős–Straus–Schinzel conjecture)

title: '3-divisible ES': 12/p fails at 22 primes ≤ 10⁵, last 12 241
why: Contains the Type-A failures 193 and 2521 and the R-zero 577: the '3-divisible' sub-problem is hard on the same primes — a sub-ES whose failure set is a fingerprint of global hardness.
first_step: Extend 12/p to 10⁷ (fast: x ∈ (p/12, p/4]) to test finiteness; check whether 66529, 409, 5569 eventually appear (they do not ≤ 10⁵ except as listed).
refs: arXiv:2511.16817 (Pomerance–Weingartner, Exceptions to the Erdős–Straus–Schinzel conjecture)

title: '4-divisible ES': 16/p last failure ≤ 10⁵ is 83449 — an R-zero
connection: 16/p failures (38 primes ≤ 10⁵) include 193, 577, 1201, 2521, 3361, 3169, 4801, 33601, 36529, 78721 and end at 83449, which is also a (★) failure.
why: Two independent hardness tests pick out the same large prime 83449: suggests a shared 2-adic obstruction (p ≡ 1 mod 16? 83449 mod 16 = 9) worth isolating.
first_step: Compute v₂(p−1), p mod 16/32/64 for all 16/p failures and for the 14 R-zeros; test whether 2-adic depth predicts both.

title: '5-divisible ES': 20/p fails at 63 primes ≤ 10⁵, last 90001
connection: No ES solution with 5 | x, y, z at 63 primes ≤ 10⁵, including 1201, 2521, 4201, 4801, 8761, 21841, 24481 (ES-hard) — the last at 90001 = 9·10⁴+1.
why: The 5-divisible failure set mirrors primes ≡ 1 (mod 5^a·…) — a local obstruction at 5 that compounds global hardness.
first_step: Tabulate p mod 25 and mod 125 for 20/p failures vs random primes.

title: Divisibility-strengthened ES_k ladder (k | x,y,z): last failures 241, 12241, 83449, 90001, ≥97777, 92401, …
why: PW prove n_m ≥ exp(m^{1/3+o(1)}), so ES_k fails infinitely far out as k grows but each ES_k plausibly has finitely many failures — a quantitative family 'between' ES and false statements, useful to calibrate any method's strength (a method proving ES_k for k=3 would be stronger than ES).
first_step: Pick the smallest k (k=2, 'even ES') and try to push the census to 10¹⁰ with a dedicated sieve; check whether the 8/n exceptions really stop at 241.
refs: arXiv:2511.16817 (Pomerance–Weingartner, Exceptions to the Erdős–Straus–Schinzel conjecture)

title: Failure sets are monotone under divisibility of the numerator (sanity + structure)
connection: If m | m′ then fail(m) ⊆ fail(m′) (multiply all denominators of an m′/n representation by m′/m to get one of m/n); verified on all m ≤ 48, p ≤ 10⁵. 'Primitive' failures (not explained by a divisor d ≥ 5 of m) number 0,0,1,6,4,8,3,22,10,8,25,32,17,45,…
why: ES is the bottom of a divisibility lattice of Schinzel problems; primitive failure counts strip out inherited obstructions and are the right 'new difficulty' per numerator.
first_step: Submit primitive-failure counts to OEIS; examine whether primitive failures of 4k concentrate on primes hard for 4/p.
refs: arXiv:2511.16817 (Pomerance–Weingartner, Exceptions to the Erdős–Straus–Schinzel conjecture)

title: Hardness index H(p) = #{m ≤ 48 : m/p fails} correlates with U(p)/log²p (ρ = −0.43)
why: A single prime-level 'obstruction profile' across numerators: if hardness were a local (Euler-product) phenomenon, H(p) should be predictable from p mod small numbers — a cheap test of locality.
first_step: Regress H(p) on Legendre symbols (q/p) for q ≤ 30 and on p mod 8,9,16,25; report R².

title: R-zeros and Type-A failures across numerators: 193 fails 19 numerators, 577 13, 2521 11, 3361 11, 409 7, 9601 5, 5569 4, 66529 3, 23929 0
connection: Among m ∈ [5,48], the campaign's hard primes fail many m/p; but 23929 (an R-zero) fails none — R-failure is not 'globally hard'.
why: Separates certificate-line hardness ((★) zeros) from intrinsic ES hardness — useful to decide which hard primes are artefacts of a chosen line.
first_step: For each of the 14 R-zeros compute U(p)/log²p and H(p) to rank 'intrinsic' vs 'line-specific' hardness.

title: PW numerics reproduced: for every m ∈ [20,48] some prime in (m², 2m²) fails m/p
connection: Counts of failing primes in (m², 2m²): m=20:6, 21:5, 22:5, 23:5, 24:13, …, 48:70 — consistent with PW's reported numerics for m ≥ 20.
why: Independent confirmation of a 2025 literature claim with our engine; and the counts per m give an empirical density to compare with PW's probabilistic model.
first_step: Compare the counts with PW's predicted number (their Elsholtz–Tao-style density) in (m², 2m²).
refs: arXiv:2511.16817 (Pomerance–Weingartner, Exceptions to the Erdős–Straus–Schinzel conjecture)

title: Prime numerators have far fewer failures than composite ones
why: Composite m inherit failures from divisors (monotonicity) but also have fewer 'cheap' identities; the prime-m sequence measures the bare Schinzel difficulty.
first_step: Fit #failures(m) for prime m vs m (power law?) and compare with PW's exp(m^{1/3}) lower bound for n_m.
refs: arXiv:2511.16817 (Pomerance–Weingartner, Exceptions to the Erdős–Straus–Schinzel conjecture)

title: 9/n fails exactly at {2,5,11,19} (≤ 10⁵ primes, n ≤ 4000)
connection: Tiny, apparently complete exception set for 9/n; 9 = 3² so 9/n relates to 3/n-type identities.
why: Small complete exception lists are the most 'fingerprintable'; no OEIS hit for {2,5,11,19} beyond spurious ones.
first_step: Prove completeness of {2,5,11,19} for 9/n by covering congruences (expected possible since 9/n has many identities) — a warm-up for the ES covering obstruction.

title: 10/n fails at {2,3,7,11,43,61,67,181}; 11/n at {2,3,4,37}; 13/n at {2,3,4,5,7,14,53,61,67,79,211,281}
connection: Complete-looking small exception lists (n ≤ 4000 all, primes ≤ 10⁵), none in OEIS; composite exceptions occur (4 for 11 and 13, 14 for 13).
why: Each list is a finite certificate target; the presence of composite exceptions (4, 14) shows the reduction-to-primes fails for m ≠ 4, unlike ES.
first_step: Explain 13/14 and 11/4 failures (why multiplicativity breaks) and check whether any composite n > 100 fails m/n for m ≤ 13.

title: 15/p failure set contains three of the 30 hardest ES primes (4201, 12601, 20521)
connection: 15/p fails at 25 primes ≤ 10⁵ ending 1103,1171,1367,4201,6301,12601,16831,20521; 4201, 12601, 20521 are top-30 hard for 4/p though 15 is not a multiple of 4.
why: Cross-numerator coincidence not explained by divisibility monotonicity; suggests a shared local cause (p ≡ 1 mod 120 or 840?).
first_step: Compute p mod 840 for 15/p failures and test enrichment of p ≡ 1 (mod 120).

title: m/p failures are enriched in primes adjacent to 5-smooth numbers
connection: For m=12, 15 of 22 failures have p−1 or p+1 5-smooth (only 182 such primes ≤ 10⁵ in total); m=20: 27/63; m=24: 39/146 — OEIS returns spurious A219669 ('primes neighboring a 5-smooth number') for m=45.
why: Primes next to smooth numbers are ≡ ±1 modulo many small numbers simultaneously — the Mordell-class mechanism; a quantitative version is a 'smooth-neighbour' hardness law.
first_step: Compute failure rate among 5-smooth-neighbour primes vs others for each m; extend to 7-smooth.

title: Last-failure sequence by numerator m (7..48) is not in OEIS
why: These are lower bounds for Schinzel's n_m (true values may be larger beyond 10⁵); a curated table would let PW-type theory be compared with data.
first_step: Extend each m to 10⁷ (cost drops ∝ 1/m) and submit as 'largest known prime p with m/p not a sum of 3 unit fractions'.
refs: arXiv:2511.16817 (Pomerance–Weingartner, Exceptions to the Erdős–Straus–Schinzel conjecture)

title: Number of m/p failures ≤ 10⁵ by m: 0,0,1,6,4,8,3,22,10,9,25,38,17,49,16,63,… (no OEIS match)
connection: The failure-count profile across m (5..48) has strong arithmetic modulation (peaks at m ≡ 0 mod 12).
why: A Fourier/arith analysis of this profile would expose which local factors (mod 3, mod 4) drive Schinzel failures.
first_step: Regress log(#fail(m)+1) on log m and the indicator functions 4|m, 3|m, 5|m.

title: U₈(p) = number of all-even ES solutions of 4/p
connection: By scaling, U₈(p) counts solutions of 4/p with x, y, z even; at primes: 0,0,1,3,0,3,0,2,7,4,12,6,…
why: Ratio U₈(p)/U₄(p) is the 'even fraction' of ES solutions — a 2-adic statistic; if it tends to a constant, even-ES is ES with a constant-factor loss.
first_step: Compute U₈(p)/U₄(p) average by p mod 8 and mod 16; compare with the 2-adic local density of the ES surface.

title: U₁₂(p)/U₄(p): the 3-divisible fraction of ES solutions
connection: U₁₂(p) counts solutions of 4/p with 3 | x,y,z; its ratio to U₄(p) is a 3-adic local statistic; failures at 193, 577, 2521 mean this fraction hits 0 at hard primes.
why: Factorisation of the count into local factors (Euler product over divisibility conditions) would be a strong structural fingerprint (Manin-type).
first_step: Compute E[U_{4k}(p)/U₄(p)] for k=2,3,5 and compare with 1/k³-type local densities on the ES surface.

title: Joint failure: no prime ≤ 10⁵ fails both 8/p and 12/p beyond {2,3}
connection: fail(8) ∩ fail(12) = {2,3}; fail(8) ∩ fail(16) = fail(8) by monotonicity; overlaps of non-nested failure sets are small.
why: Different divisibility strengthenings fail on disjoint primes; a covering-by-subfamilies proof (each prime gets an even OR 3-divisible solution) is numerically plausible: 'ES_2 ∪ ES_3 covers all p > 3'.
first_step: Verify 'every prime p > 3 has an ES solution with all-even or all-3-divisible denominators' to 10⁷, and find the minimal such union family.

title: A union conjecture: ES_2 ∪ ES_3 (even or 3-divisible solutions) for all primes p > 3
connection: Since fail(8) ∩ fail(12) ∩ primes = {2,3} ≤ 10⁵, conjecture: every prime p > 3 has an ES solution with 2 | x,y,z or 3 | x,y,z.
why: Each subfamily has a cleaner local structure (2-adic resp. 3-adic) than ES; a proof could exploit that the obstructions live at different primes (analogous to López's Type A ∪ Type B conjecture).
first_step: Extend the joint census; search for the natural certificate lines in each subfamily and check whether their failure sets are disjoint.

title: Composite-n failures for m ≤ 13 are only 4, 14, 25
connection: Among n ≤ 4000, the composite failures of m/n for 5 ≤ m ≤ 13 are n = 4 (m=11,13), 14 (m=13), 25 (m=12) — tiny.
why: For ES (m=4) composites reduce to primes; for m ≥ 5 they almost do: suggests a near-multiplicative structure of solvability.
first_step: Prove: if m/p solvable for each prime p | n then m/n solvable except finitely many n (check 25 for m=12: 12/5 solvable? no — so it's inherited).

title: 12/25 fails while 12/5 fails: inherited, but 13/14 fails with 13/2, 13/7 failing
connection: Composite failures appear to be products of failing primes (25 = 5², 14 = 2·7, 4 = 2²): consistent with 'fail(m/n) ⇒ each prime factor fails or is tiny'.
why: If 'n fails ⇒ every prime factor of n fails' held for all m it would reduce Schinzel to primes as for ES.
first_step: Test the implication on m ≤ 48 and n ≤ 4000 composite (needs composite runs for m > 13).

title: Hardest-for-15 vs hardest-for-4: correlation across numerators
connection: Compute Spearman between U₄(p)/log²p and U_m(p)/log²p for each m ≤ 48 (data on disk).
why: If hardness is one latent arithmetic variable (e.g. L(1,χ_p) and p−1 smoothness), correlations should be high for all m and highest for m sharing factors with 840.
first_step: Run the 44 correlations; cluster m by correlation profile.

title: Schinzel sibling with j unit fractions (PW's generalisation)
connection: PW also treat m/n as a sum of j unit fractions; the analogous fingerprints (failure sets of m/n with j=2,3,4) give a two-parameter table.
why: The j=2 case is purely divisor-theoretic (m/n = 1/x+1/y ⟺ divisors of n² in a class) — an exactly solvable layer whose failure statistics calibrate j=3.
first_step: Note 4/n = 1/x + 1/y is solvable iff n is even or has a prime factor ≡ 3 (mod 4), so its exceptional set (all prime factors ≡ 1 mod 4) has density zero — the same set as the isosceles-law failures; compute and the j=4 exceptions for m ≤ 48.
refs: arXiv:2511.16817 (Pomerance–Weingartner, Exceptions to the Erdős–Straus–Schinzel conjecture)

title: Explicit check of PW's 'prime in (m², 2m²)' theorem threshold
connection: PW prove the existence of a failing prime in (m², 2m²) for m ≥ 6.52·10⁹ and observe it numerically from m ≥ 20; our census confirms m=20..48.
why: Their mechanism (Elsholtz–Tao divisor sums with p near m²) is a lower-bound-on-failures argument; its ES analogue is what the campaign's 'no-go' items should respect: such arguments cannot prove ES because m=4 is fixed.
first_step: Read PW §§3–4 and write down where m → ∞ is used; check whether any of it says something about fixed m=4 (it shouldn't).
refs: arXiv:2511.16817 (Pomerance–Weingartner, Exceptions to the Erdős–Straus–Schinzel conjecture)

title: Primes failing ≥ 15 numerators are all < 700
connection: High H(p) occurs only at small p (113, 193, 101, 137, 181, 421, 149, 241, 281, 353, 397, …); for p > 10⁴, H(p) is small.
why: Shows that 'multi-numerator hardness' decays with p — consistent with Vaughan-type almost-all results with explicit m-dependence (PW).
first_step: Plot max H(p) over dyadic ranges.

title: 8/n failures 131 and 241 vs ES hardness of 131 (≡ 3 mod 4) and 241
connection: 241 is a top-30 hard prime for 4/p and the last 8/p failure; 131 ≡ 3 (mod 4) is easy for 4/p.
why: Mixed picture: the even-ES failures are not explained by 4/p hardness alone; 131 needs a separate 2-adic explanation.
first_step: Examine all ES solutions of 4/131 and why none has all-even denominators (parity of x,y,z patterns).

title: Last 16/p failure 83449 and last 12/p failure 12241: next-term prediction
connection: If ES_k failure sets are finite, the largest elements grow quickly with k; PW-type heuristics would predict last(ES_k) ≈ exp(c k^{1/3}) or similar.
why: A cheap predictive check of the probabilistic model behind PW on the ES-relevant numerators 4k.
first_step: Fit log last(4k) for k = 2..5 and compare with PW's density model; extend 16/p and 20/p to 10⁷ to see if new failures appear.
refs: arXiv:2511.16817 (Pomerance–Weingartner, Exceptions to the Erdős–Straus–Schinzel conjecture)

title: Word sieve reproduces every campaign census (cheap independent engine)
connection: A 25-line C sieve over n = tuv − u − v (all n ≤ 3·10⁶ in 5 s) reproduces the 114 I3 zeros (max 2 433 600), the R-zeros ≤ 3·10⁶, and the six non-square U failures ≤ 10⁶.
why: A third independent engine for the censuses; also makes per-n counts (not just zero sets) available for fingerprinting.
first_step: Extend to 3·10⁸ with uint16 counters in a memory-bounded segmented version and re-certify the (★) census to that height.

title: All I3 zeros > 50 that are odd: 55, 59, 83, 87, 103, 105, 119, 143, 145, 159, 175, 1225
connection: Of the 114 I3 zeros only 12 odd ones exceed 50, the last being 1225 = 35²; even zeros go up to 2 433 600 = 1560².
why: The odd/even split suggests I3 restricted to odd n has a much smaller exceptional set — a cleaner conjecture ('every odd n > 1225 is tuv−u−v with t,u,v ≥ 3') for p-relevant n.
first_step: State and record the odd-I3 conjecture with census to 3·10⁶; check whether odd I3 suffices for the ES application (primes are odd).

title: I3 zero squares: 1,4,…,1225,1600,19600,2 433 600
why: Squares are over-represented among late I3 zeros, echoing T1 (odd squares kill all certificate lines). A T1-like reciprocity for even squares with I3 would explain 19600 and 2433600.
first_step: Compute I3(m²) for m ≤ 3000 and check whether I3(m²) is systematically small (but nonzero) for m divisible by 4·3·5·…

title: 2 433 600 = 1560² is a zero of I3, R, Uv and ESC simultaneously
connection: At n = 1560² every certificate family in the word sieve vanishes (W = 54 but I3 = R = Uv = ESC = 0); same at 1225 = 35² and 105.
why: The largest I3 zero is a square with smooth root; suggests the I3 exceptional set is 'squares with smooth roots + small n' — directly testable.
first_step: Test I3(m²) for smooth m (m = 2^a3^b5^c13^d…) up to 10⁸ via a targeted solver for tuv−u−v = m².

title: 105 = 3·5·7 is a zero of I3, R, Uv and ESC
connection: n = 105 is the first non-square zero of the U family and also an I3, (★) and 'some coordinate in 4ℤ∪(8ℤ−n)' zero; ES(105) holds via other identities.
why: 105 is the smallest n where all word-type certificate lines fail outside squares — a minimal counterexample to 'words cover all odd n ≡ 1 (4)' and a test case for any new certificate family.
first_step: List all ES solutions of 4/105 and classify which structural family produces each.

title: ESC zero set: non-squares are 105, 288, 336, 672, 1380, 29568, 41220, 57696, 97440, 255360, …, 2 402 400
connection: n with no word having a coordinate in 4ℤ ∪ (8ℤ − n): only 105 among odd non-squares ≤ 3·10⁶; the even ones are highly smooth (2402400 = 2⁵·3·5²·7·11·13).
why: The even zeros are irrelevant for ES but are a clean 'smooth-number obstruction' fingerprint of the same word equation.
first_step: Check whether even ESC zeros are exactly the n with n+1 and 2n+1 having no divisors in the required classes (characterise).

title: R(n) = 0 at n = 2^k − 1 for k ∈ {2,3,4,5,7,8,13}
connection: The (★) count vanishes at 3, 7, 15, 31, 127, 255, 8191 although R(n) = 0 has density < 0.1% among n ≡ 3 (mod 8); R(2^k−1) > 0 for other k ≤ 21.
why: Mersenne numbers are 'p-tied' obstructions: 4C(2^k − 1) + 1 = 2^{k+2}C − 4C + 1 has restricted divisor classes; a cute but real fingerprint for the divisor form of R.
first_step: Explain via the divisor form R(n) = Σ_C #{d | 4Cn+1 : d ≡ −1 (mod 4C)} with n = 2^k − 1; test R(2^k − 1) for k ≤ 61 with a dedicated divisor search.

title: R(3^k) = 0 exactly for even k (squares) and k = 1
why: Sanity fingerprint of T1 on prime powers; also the odd-power values (2,2,4,18,10,10) are a small test sequence for any closed formula.
first_step: Compare R(3^{2j+1}) with the BM main term M_BM(3^{2j+1}).

title: R-zeros among odd non-squares: 3,7,15,31,39,51,57,79,99,105,127,177,199,249,255,291,295,345,387,409,…
connection: Not in OEIS; for n ≡ 1 (8) R=0 has frequency 0.30%, n ≡ 5 (8) exactly 0 (≤ 3·10⁶), n ≡ 3,7 (8) ≈ 0.05%.
why: R ≡ 0 is impossible at n ≡ 5 (8) in range — is there a proof (an identity in the (★) family covering n ≡ 5 mod 8)? Such class-level proofs are the template for covering arguments.
first_step: Prove R(n) ≥ 1 for n ≡ 5 (mod 8) (look for an explicit (u,B,C) family), and similarly U(n) ≥ 1 for n ≡ 3,5,7 (mod 8) (Uv zero rate is exactly 0 there).

title: Composite R-zeros include the pseudosquare 2641 = 19·139
connection: Composite non-square n ≡ 1 (4) with R(n) = 0: 57, 105, 177, 249, 345, 465, 777, 801, 969, 1345, 1465, 1617, …, 2641, …; 2641 is Lehmer's pseudosquare L₁₃ (A002189) and also an x=(n+3)/4 greedy failure.
why: Pseudosquares mimic squares for all small-prime Legendre symbols; T1 kills squares, so pseudosquares should be near-T1 — a quantitative 'approximate reciprocity obstruction'.
first_step: Compute R, U, Uv, I3 at all pseudosquares A002189 up to 10¹⁰ (targeted divisor-form computation) and compare with typical values.

title: Pseudosquares as approximate squares for T1: a conjecture
connection: Conjecture: for pseudosquares L_q (QR mod all primes ≤ q, ≡ 1 mod 8), every certificate-line count is ≪ (small) and tends to vanish as q grows, i.e. T1 is 'approximately' active.
why: Would identify the arithmetic source of the hardest ES instances and give a family where any proof must use large-prime information.
first_step: Test on A002189 terms up to 10¹² using R's divisor form (only C ≤ few hundred needed for a lower bound on R).

title: Mean R(n)/log²n on n ≡ 1 (4) drifts 0.145 → 0.133 (10³ → 10⁶)
connection: Average of R(n)/(log n)² over n ≡ 1 (4) in [X, 2X]: 0.1446 (10³), 0.1388 (10⁴), 0.1353 (10⁵), 0.1332 (10⁶); FRONTIER lists constants 1/8 = 0.125 (all integers) and 3/(2π²) = 0.152.
why: Drift towards 1/8 with a 1/log correction is a sharp numerical test of the second-order term in the (★) mean.
first_step: Fit mean = 1/8 + a/log X + b/log²X to 10⁸; compare with a second-order term from the divisor-sum asymptotics.

title: BM main term explains the ES count U(p) better than its own (★) count
connection: At 696 primes p≡1(4) ≤ 12 000: residual Spearman(M_BM, U) = +0.65 but residual Spearman(M_BM, R) = +0.10; raw Spearman(R, M_BM) = 0.47 (shared log² growth); mean R/M_BM = 1.31.
why: M_BM is built from χ_p(uB) so it tracks the χ_p Euler product that drives U; R's fluctuations follow χ_{−4p} instead — the BM layer is not the dominant fluctuation term of R, a mismatch worth understanding.
first_step: Recompute on 20 000–30 000 (running: data/z52b/bm_check_20000_30000.json) and decompose R(p) − M_BM(p) into higher-order characters (the X(n) part of FRONTIER §2.1).

title: R-zeros sit in the low tail of M_BM but not at its bottom
why: A small BM main term is neither necessary nor sufficient for R(p) = 0 — the fluctuation term X(p) (characters of order ≥ 3) matters; quantifies how much a pure-BM argument can miss.
first_step: For each R-zero compute the full character decomposition M_gen and X; record which characters cancel the main term.

title: (★) and Uv and I3 zero rates by n mod 8
why: Concentration of all failures in n ≡ 1 (8) mirrors ES's Mordell structure; any line with failures at n ≡ 3,7 (8) carries extra, avoidable difficulty.
first_step: Tabulate zero rates by n mod 24 and mod 840 for each family; find the family whose zero set is contained in the square classes mod 840.

title: I3(n) = 1 is rare beyond 1000: 2160, 2316, 3900, 9090, 9408, 30276, 453660
connection: Only seven n in (1000, 3·10⁶] have exactly one I3 word.
why: The single-word survivors are 'almost-zeros'; their structure (all even, smooth) predicts where a hypothetical further I3 zero would lie.
first_step: Factor them (2160 = 2⁴3³5, 453660 = 2²·3·5·7561, 7561 prime) and look for a common shape with 2433600.

title: W(n) (all words) has records at 1,3,5,7,11,17,19,23,35,47,59,71,…
connection: Records of W(n) = #{t,u,v ≥ 1 : tuv−u−v = n} are at n with n+1 and 2n+1, 3n+1… all highly divisible (W counts divisors of tn+1 in classes); not in OEIS.
why: W(n) = Σ_t #{d | tn+1 : d ≡ −1 (mod t)} is the unrestricted analogue of the ES certificate count — its extremal behaviour bounds all sub-counts.
first_step: Identify W(n) with a classical divisor-sum (Σ_t τ_{−1 mod t}(tn+1)); submit to OEIS.

title: t=1 and t=2 word counts are τ(n+1) and τ(2n+1) (OEIS A000005, A099774)
connection: The t=1 slice of tuv−u−v=n is (u−1)(v−1)=n+1 → τ(n+1); the t=2 slice is (2u−1)(2v−1)=2n+1 → τ(2n+1) (OEIS confirmed).
why: Sanity anchor for the word sieve, and a reminder that each t-slice is a divisor function of tn+1 restricted to −1 mod t — the 'tied-modulus divisor event'.
first_step: None (anchor); use as unit tests.

title: R(p) is always even — the (u,B) swap involution
connection: R(p) at primes p≡1(4): 2,2,2,4,2,6,4,4,2,8,…, always even (FRONTIER notes it); R(p)/2 = #{u<B}.
why: R(p)/2 is the natural 'unordered' count; parity information beyond this (R(p)/2 mod 2) could come from a second involution as in Zagier's proof.
first_step: Check the distribution of R(p)/2 mod 2 by p mod 8; search for a second involution on (★) triples with computable fixed points.

title: U failure set vs I3 zero set: only 105 is common
connection: The U failures {105, 2961, 3985, 25305, 111969, 978145} and the I3 zeros intersect only in 105.
why: Different word restrictions fail on nearly disjoint sets — union arguments (U ∪ I3 covers all n ≡ 1 (4) except squares and 105?) are numerically plausible.
first_step: Compute the joint zero set of U and I3 among n ≡ 1 (4), n ≤ 3·10⁶; state a union conjecture.

title: Joint zeros of R and Uv among n ≡ 1 (4)
connection: Since R (t ∈ 4ℤ) and Uv (v ∈ 𝒞_n) are different slices of the same word equation, their joint zero set among n≡1(4) non-squares should be tiny.
why: A two-line union covering all primes is the most economical certificate statement; FRONTIER notes (★) ∪ b=1 never fails ≤ 10⁸.
first_step: Compute the joint zero set of (R, Uv) and of (R, I3) ≤ 3·10⁶ from words_3e6.npy.

title: ESC(p) as a certificate count at primes — calibrate ESC(p)/log²p
connection: ESC(p) (words with some coordinate in 4ℤ ∪ (8ℤ−p)) is existence-equivalent to ES at primes per CONTEXT, but it is a count of certificates, not a lower bound for the number of solutions (ESC(5) = 6 > U(5) = 2); its residual follows χ_p with α ≈ −0.24 (R²-gain 0.31).
why: If ESC(p)/log²p is bounded below empirically with a cleaner constant than U, it is the better target count for lower-bound heuristics.
first_step: Compute min_{p ∈ [X,2X]} ESC(p)/log²p up to 3·10⁶ and compare its stability to U(p)'s.

title: R(p) correlates with τ(4p+1)? — divisor-form check
connection: R(p) = Σ_C #{d | 4Cp+1 : d ≡ −1 (mod 4C)}; the C=1 term is #{d | 4p+1 : d ≡ 3 (mod 4)}; minz(p)/p correlates −0.42 with τ(4p+1).
why: Quantifies how much of R comes from C = 1 — if most, the (★) problem is essentially about one integer 4p+1 (a 'single shifted prime' divisor problem).
first_step: Compute the C-profile of R(p): fraction of R from C = 1, 2, 3, … at p ≤ 10⁶.

title: Distribution of the smallest C in (★) certificates
connection: For each p with R(p) > 0, Cmin(p) = least C contributing; its distribution (geometric? power law?) is a fingerprint of how 'far' the certificate is.
why: Bounded Cmin would be a finite covering; growth of max Cmin(p) over p ≤ X measures the needed modulus range.
first_step: Compute Cmin(p) for p ≤ 3·10⁶ via a C-major sieve and fit max_{p≤X} Cmin(p).

title: I3(p) at primes: 31, 43, 47, 59, 83, 103 are zeros
connection: I3(p) = 0 at small primes 31, 43, 47, 59, 83, 103; none beyond 103 (odd zeros > 103 are composite: 105, 119, 143, 145, 159, 175, 1225).
why: I3 restricted to primes has exceptional set {…,103}: a candidate 'I3 for primes' theorem target with a tiny exception list.
first_step: State 'every prime p > 103 is tuv−u−v with t,u,v ≥ 3' with census to 3·10⁶; look for a covering-congruence proof for p ≡ 1 (4).

title: Uv zero set (all residues): 12, 28, 60, 96, 105, 124, 156, 204, 228, 288, …, 2961, …
connection: Without the n ≡ 1 (4) restriction, U-zeros are mostly even (multiples of 4 with n+1 prime-ish); non-OEIS.
why: Restricting the certificate condition to n ≡ 1 (4) loses nothing; the even zeros are an artefact — clarifies scope of U.
first_step: None beyond recording; possibly characterise the even zeros as n with n+v having no divisor ≡ −1 (mod v) for every allowed v.

title: Greedy failures (no solution with x = ⌈(n+1)/4⌉) at composites: 1729 (taxicab) and 2641 (pseudosquare)
why: 1729 = 7·13·19 and 2641 = 19·139 are both products of primes ≡ 1 (mod 6) or with special QR profile; probably coincidence, but cheap to test whether greedy failures are closed under multiplication.
first_step: Check: are greedy failures exactly the n ≡ 1 (24) all of whose 'x=(n+3)/4 divisor pairs' are blocked mod 3 — derive and test closure.

title: A segmented word sieve to 10¹⁰ for per-n counts
connection: The word sieve is O(N log²N); a segmented version (block in n, loop over (t,u) with v-range intersecting the block) gives counts to 10¹⁰ in hours.
why: Per-n counts (not only zero sets) at large heights allow fingerprinting the minimum count growth, the true test of any log²-lower-bound conjecture.
first_step: Implement segmented z52b_fingerprint_words with uint8 saturating counters for I3, R, Uv; run to 10¹⁰ on primes p≡1(4) only.

title: min over p ≤ X of R(p)/log²p: does it go to 0?
connection: R has 14 zeros ≤ 10¹⁰, so inf R/log²p = 0 infinitely often is possible; the empirical lower envelope of R(p)/log²p over primes with R > 0 is a separate fingerprint.
why: If the positive values are bounded below by c·log²p while zeros persist, failures are 'discrete' events (local obstructions) rather than tail events of a smooth distribution — matters for which probabilistic model to use.
first_step: Histogram R(p)/log²p near 0 (values 2, 4, 6) for p ≤ 3·10⁶ and compare with Poisson with the BM mean.

title: Poisson test for R(p) given M_BM(p)
connection: If R(p) ≈ Poisson-like with mean ∝ M_BM(p), P(R=0) ≈ exp(−c M_BM) — at M_BM ≈ 3 (p=409) this gives a few % — test against the 14 observed zeros.
why: Calibrates the 'tied-modulus divisor event' independence model of FRONTIER §2.1 against actual zero counts.
first_step: Fit P(R=0 | M_BM) by logistic regression on p ≤ 3·10⁶ (needs M_BM for all p; use the script with chunking).

title: Higher-power residue characters of 2,3,5,7 have no detectable effect on ES counts
connection: Within strata of fixed quadratic profile ((2/p),(3/p),(5/p),(7/p)), whether a ∈ {2,3,5,7} is a cubic/quartic/octic residue mod p shifts mean residual log U(p), k₁, k₂, R(p) by |Δ| ≤ 0.03 (largest −0.029; the attached Mann–Whitney p-values are unstratified tests, smallest 0.015 among 48 tests — consistent with null after multiple testing).
why: Data counterpart of the genus/higher-character split (FRONTIER §2.1): order ≥ 3 characters at small primes don't bias counts; all systematic arithmetic dependence is quadratic (plus p−1 structure).
first_step: Repeat with characters of order 3,4 of larger moduli (q ≤ 50) and with the full X(n) decomposition on (★).

title: 2-adic depth matters: p ≡ 1 (16) has 9% fewer ES solutions than p ≡ 9 (16)
connection: Among p ≡ 1 (8), residual log U(p) is lower by 0.094 when p ≡ 1 (16) (k₁ −0.098, k₂ −0.080, R −0.051); next level 32 vs 16 only −0.013; 9 vs 3: −0.030; 25 vs 5: −0.021.
why: Not explained by quadratic characters ((2/p) = 1 in both classes) nor by the quartic character of 2 (null): it is the multiplicative depth of p−1 at 2 — local densities of the ES surface at 2 depend on p mod 16.
first_step: Compute the 2-adic local density of {4/p = 1/x+1/y+1/z} as a function of p mod 2^k and compare to the observed 9% gap.

title: Quartic residuosity of 2 (p = x² + 64y²) is irrelevant for ES counts
connection: Among p ≡ 1 (8), '2 is a 4th power mod p' shifts residual log U by +0.008 (MW p = 0.10).
why: Rules out a tempting Gauss-type link (p = x²+64y²) to hardness; the Neumann–Setzer form p = u²+64 is a different condition (see next item).
first_step: None needed; record as negative fingerprint.

title: Neumann–Setzer primes p = u² + 64 among hard primes?
connection: For prime conductor p ≠ 17, elliptic curves with a rational 2-torsion point exist iff p = u² + 64 (Neumann–Setzer; conductor 17 is the exception, LMFDB 17.a); check whether ES-hard primes or R-zeros are of this form (e.g. 409 − 64 = 345 is not a square; 577 − 64 = 513 not).
why: LMFDB fingerprint: an ES ↔ elliptic-curve-of-conductor-p link would show up as over-representation of p = u²+64 among hard primes.
first_step: Test all 14 R-zeros, 3 Type-A failures and the 40 hardest primes for p = u²+64; and correlate U(p) with #isogeny classes of conductor p in LMFDB.

title: Number of elliptic curves of conductor p (or 4p, 8p, 16p) vs U(p)
connection: LMFDB lists curves by conductor; their number at N = p, 2p, 4p, 8p, 16p could correlate with ES counts if ES surfaces fibre into genus-1 curves (cf. GEOMETRY_ES.md) of these conductors.
why: Fibrations of the ES cubic surface by conics/genus-1 curves have discriminants involving p; the Mordell–Weil ranks of such fibres might govern solution counts.
first_step: Download LMFDB conductor counts for N ≤ 500 000 (Cremona tables) and correlate with U(p) residual at p ≤ 30 000 (N=16p).

title: Ranks of the genus-1 fibres of the ES surface at hard primes
connection: Fixing one denominator turns 4/p = 1/x+1/y+1/z into a conic; fixing a linear relation gives cubic curves. Compute the Mordell–Weil rank of natural elliptic fibres for p ∈ {193, 409, 577, 2521, 66529} vs easy primes.
why: If hard primes correlate with rank-0 fibres, a Mordell–Weil/Selmer viewpoint would be a new lever (rank parity via root numbers is computable).
first_step: Construct a genuine genus-one fibration of the ES cubic surface (note: the substitution x = ty only gives conics 4tyz = p(ty + (t+1)z); use e.g. a pencil of plane sections through a line on the surface or a non-linear pencil) and compute ranks with Sage/Magma at the listed p.

title: U(p) residual vs Σ_{d≤8} τ(p+4d) is null (ρ = +0.02)
connection: The b = 1 (López Type A) line asks for a divisor of p+4d ≡ −1 (mod 4d); yet the raw divisor mass Σ_{d≤8} τ(p+4d) is uncorrelated with U(p), while τ((p+3)/4) correlates +0.59.
why: Divisor *mass* of shifts is not what matters — the residue-class restriction is; shows why naive divisor-sum lower bounds don't track solvability.
first_step: Replace τ by the class-restricted count #{e | p+4d : e ≡ −1 (4d)} and recompute.

title: τ(p+1) and τ(p+4) correlate weakly (+0.12), τ(p+12) not at all
connection: Shifted divisor functions at shifts 1,4,12 carry little information on ES count, unlike shift 3 (+0.48 for τ(p+3)).
why: Highlights the special role of the shift 3 (x = (p+3)/4), i.e. the first greedy step, among all shifts.
first_step: Tabulate ρ(U, τ(p+s)) for s = 1..50 to find the full 'shift spectrum' and compare with which x-values carry solutions.

title: k₂ (Type II) is more sensitive to 3 than k₁: ρ((3/p)) = −0.41 vs −0.25
connection: Residual k₂(p) correlates −0.41 with (3/p) and −0.39 with v₃(p−1); k₁(p) correlates −0.25 and −0.25.
why: Type II solutions come from divisors of p-tied integers in classes mod 4C; C = 3 multiples are cheap — p ≡ 2 (mod 3) helps Type II most.
first_step: Count Type II solutions by C (the c=1 parameter) and check which C carry the 3-dependence.

title: k₁ (Type I) is more sensitive to 5 than k₂: ρ((5/p)) = −0.32 for k₁
connection: Residual k₁ correlates −0.32 with (5/p); k₂ less (not in top list).
why: Different local primes drive the two types; designing a covering argument per type should exploit their complementary local profiles.
first_step: Build a table ρ(type, (q/p)) for q ≤ 50 and both types.

title: k₂ correlates with spf(p+4) (−0.35)
connection: Smallest prime factor of p+4 anticorrelates with k₂(p): p+4 with small factors → more Type II solutions.
why: p+4 = 4·((p+3)/4)+1… p+4 divisors are the b=1, d=1 line; small factors give many small divisors in classes ≡ −1 (mod 4C).
first_step: Check ρ(k₂, spf(p+4C)) for C = 1..10.

title: minz(p)/p anticorrelates with h(−4p)/√p (−0.19)
connection: The cheapest certificate is lower (smaller height) when L(1,χ_{−4p}) is large.
why: Height of the optimal solution relates to the (★)/Type II side (χ_{−4p}); a height bound and an L-value bound may be linked.
first_step: Regress log(minz(p)/p) on log L(1,χ_{−4p}) and log L(1,χ_p).

title: U(p) vs CF period of √p (ρ = −0.27)
connection: Longer CF period of √p (larger regulator) ⇒ fewer ES solutions.
why: ES has continued-fraction reformulations (ES₅, λ(p) ≤ 3); the CF of √p is a different object, but the correlation goes through L(1,χ_p) = 2hR/√p.
first_step: Partial correlation of U with CF period controlling for L(1,χ_p); if ≈ 0, the CF of √p carries nothing extra.

title: Real class number h(p) is uncorrelated with U(p) (−0.04)
connection: Since h(p) = 1 for most p ≡ 1 (4) at this size, only the regulator carries the L-value; h(p) alone is uninformative.
why: Negative fingerprint: avoids chasing 'class group of Q(√p)' explanations.
first_step: None.

title: r₃(p) = 12 h(−4p) for p ≡ 1 (4): ES counts vs sums of three squares
connection: By Gauss, r₃(p) = 12h(−4p) at p ≡ 1 (mod 4); so U's weak correlation with h(−4p) (+0.08 raw, +0.14 normalised) is also its correlation with r₃(p).
why: THREE_SQUARES.md explored ES ↔ ternary forms; data say the three-squares count is only a weak predictor — the right ternary form, if any, is not x²+y²+z².
first_step: Correlate U(p) with representation numbers of other ternary forms of small discriminant (genus theory via Hurwitz numbers H(4p), H(8p), H(3p)).

title: Which ternary quadratic form's r_Q(p) best predicts U(p)?
connection: Compute-and-check: for all reduced positive ternary forms Q of discriminant ≤ 200, compute r_Q(p) at p ≡ 1 (4) ≤ 10⁵ and the Spearman with U(p) residual.
why: If some Q stands out, ES counts might be (asymptotically) a theta coefficient — the Kudla/Siegel–Weil route (KUDLA_ES.md).
first_step: Use pari qfrep on the Brandt–Intrau list (discriminant ≤ 200) and rank by correlation.

title: Hurwitz class numbers H(4p), H(8p), H(3p) jointly vs ES counts
connection: Hurwitz numbers are coefficients of weight-3/2 Eisenstein series; a linear combination of H(dp)/√p could match the χ-twist dependence found for k₁/k₂.
why: Would give a modular-form 'shadow' of the ES main term, testable to high precision.
first_step: Fit log k₂ on log H(4p)/√p, log H(8p)/√p, log H(3p)/√p; inspect coefficients for rational structure.

title: Gaussian angle of p = a² + b² is irrelevant (ρ = −0.016)
connection: min(a,b)/√p for p = a²+b² shows no correlation with U(p).
why: The Hecke angle (Gaussian-integer argument) is the Kubilius/Hecke-character analogue; its irrelevance says Hecke Grössencharacters of Q(i) don't modulate ES counts.
first_step: Also test cos(4θ_p), cos(8θ_p) for the Hecke characters of Q(i) (Kubilius) — expect null.

title: Root numbers / L-functions of quadratic twists of 32a1 by p
connection: Compute-and-check: the twist E^{(p)}: py² = x³ − x (congruent-number-type curve) has root number determined by p mod 8; its analytic rank at hard primes vs others.
why: Congruent-number style curves are the classic 'Diophantine via elliptic curves' fingerprint; ES hardness clustered in p ≡ 1 (8) where these twists have root number +1.
first_step: Use pari ellanalyticrank on twists for p ≡ 1 (8) ≤ 10⁴, correlate rank with U(p)/log²p.

title: ord_p(2)/(p−1) correlates +0.45 with U(p)
connection: Higher multiplicative order of 2 mod p ⇒ more solutions; partly via (2/p) (2 is a QNR ⇒ index odd…), partly via p−1 smoothness.
why: Artin-type data (order of 2) is a cheap proxy that might enter ES via 2-power denominators (TWO_POWER_LADDER.md).
first_step: Partial correlation controlling for (2/p) and τ(p−1); compare with ord_p(3), ord_p(5).

title: R-zeros: least QNR and L(1,χ_p) are high (11 of 14 above the 85th percentile)
why: (★) failures sit where small primes are QRs mod p — the same axis as U-hardness — even though R's own fluctuations fit χ_{−4p} better; zeros are an extreme-tail event of the χ_p axis.
first_step: Logistic model P(R(p)=0) vs log L(1,χ_p) and log L(1,χ_{−4p}) on p ≤ 3·10⁶ (12 zeros) — check both coefficients' signs.

title: R-zeros have small h(−4p): 13 of 14 below the median (nominal binomial tail ≈ 0.0009)
why: Confirms the χ_{−4p} fit's prediction: (★)-hard primes have small class number of Q(√−p); the extreme version (Siegel-zero-like L(1,χ_{−4p})) would be the hardest (★) instances — ties the campaign's Siegel-dichotomy memo to data.
first_step: Extend to R-zeros beyond 10¹⁰ if the census is extended; compute the joint (h(−4p), L(1,χ_p)) quantile and see whether R-zeros are extreme in the joint distribution.

title: Type-A failures: 193 has h(−4p) in the bottom 2%, 2521 and 66529 have L(1,χ_p) at the 95th percentile
connection: 193: least QNR 5, h(−4p) quantile 0.019, L(1,χ_p) quantile 0.56; 2521: least QNR 11, L quantile 0.95; 66529: least QNR 13, L quantile 0.95.
why: Type A hardness looks χ_p-driven at 2521, 66529 but 193 is a χ_{−4p} (small class number) case — the two mechanisms both occur among the three Type-A failures.
first_step: Compute both quantiles for all Type-A near-failures (primes where the b=1 line has exactly 1–2 certificates) ≤ 10⁸.

title: Two-twist model: hardness for union (★) ∪ Type A needs both χ_p and χ_{−4p} small/large
connection: If (★) fails when L(1,χ_{−4p}) is small and Type A fails when L(1,χ_p) is large, both failing requires an unusual joint profile of (q/p) and (−1/q)(q/p) — i.e. (−1/q) = −1 primes q ≡ 3 (4) behaving oppositely.
why: Gives a heuristic reason the union never fails ≤ 10⁸ (FRONTIER §2.1) and a quantitative joint-tail prediction.
first_step: Estimate P(both lines fail) under a model where log R and log A are linear in the two log L's with fitted noise; compare with the (zero) observed count.

title: Euler-product weights per prime q for log U(p)
connection: Fit log U(p) residual = Σ_q β_q χ_p(q) for q ≤ 50 (at p ≡ 1 (4), χ_{−4p}(q) = (−1/q)χ_p(q) is collinear, so a joint χ_p/χ_{−4p} per-q fit is unidentifiable — only one coefficient per q is meaningful).
why: The fitted β_q, γ_q profile is a 'local-density fingerprint' that a heuristic count (Elsholtz–Tao style) should reproduce exactly; mismatches pinpoint missing local factors.
first_step: Done in data/z52b/qweights.json (χ_p only); compare β_q with −c/q (naive Euler factor slope).

title: Elsholtz–Tao normalisation: average U(p) grows like log³p, not log²p
connection: ET (arXiv:1107.1010, verified abstract) prove N log²N ≪ Σ_{p≤N} f(p) ≪ N log²N log log N (f ordered), i.e. average f(p) ≍ log³p up to log log; our median U(p)/log²p rises 1.33 (p≈10⁶) → 1.54 (p≈10⁷), ratio ≈ log-ratio 1.17, consistent with log³.
why: All hardness rankings across different sizes should use U(p)/log³p (or the fitted Euler-product model); the log² normalisation in several items here is only valid within a narrow range.
first_step: Refit min/median of U(p)/log³p and U(p)/(log³p·loglog p) over dyadic ranges 10³…10⁸ to see which normalisation is flat.

title: Variance of log U(p) after removing the χ_p effect: what is left?
connection: After the Euler-product fit (R² gain ≈ 0.49), the remaining residual variance can be tested against τ((p+3)/4), τ(p−1), and pure noise.
why: Quantifies how much of ES count fluctuation is 'genuinely global' (divisor coincidences) vs local — the global part is what any proof must control pointwise.
first_step: Fit the full model log U ~ log p + Euler(χ_p) + Euler(χ_{−4p}) + log τ((p+3)/4) + log τ(p−1) and report residual variance.

title: Is U(p)/log²p approximately lognormal?
connection: Histogram the residual; tails determine the probability of U(p)=0 under a smooth model — heavy lower tail would make finitely-many-exceptions heuristics fragile.
why: LOWER_TAIL_* memos study the lower tail of (★); the same for U is cheap here.
first_step: Fit normal/skew-normal to the residual and compute the predicted P(U(p) ≤ 5) vs observed (only p ≤ 17).

title: Least primitive root vs U: ρ = −0.57 (proxy check)
connection: The least primitive root g(p) is a QNR, so g(p) ≥ least QNR; its correlation is weaker than least QNR (−0.66).
why: Proxy relationship; recorded to avoid double-counting in multi-feature models.
first_step: Partial correlation of U with g(p) given least QNR.

title: ρ(U, I3(p)) = +0.46, ρ(U, W(p)) = +0.32
connection: Word counts at the same prime predict the ES count moderately; I3 more than all words.
why: I3 words (t,u,v ≥ 3) are a 'bulk' certificate family; strong correlation means I3 sees most of the arithmetic driving U.
first_step: Check whether I3(p) also follows χ_p (it does weakly: α ≈ −0.12) and whether its residual is mostly noise.

title: ES hardness vs Wieferich-type / Fermat-quotient data
connection: Compute-and-check: correlation of U(p) with q_p(2) = (2^{p−1} − 1)/p mod p (Fermat quotient) — a p-adic invariant of 2.
why: Would test whether p-adic (mod p²) information about small primes affects ES; expected null, but cheap and a clean negative.
first_step: Compute q_p(2) mod p for p ≤ 2·10⁵, normalise to [0,1), Spearman with residual U.

title: ES counts at Sophie Germain / safe primes
connection: Safe primes (p = 2q+1) have p−1 maximally non-smooth; predicted to be ES-easy. Compute mean U(p)/log²p over safe primes vs all primes ≡ 3 (mod 4) (safe primes > 7 are ≡ 3 (mod 4)… so compare within class).
why: Tests the p−1 smoothness axis independent of p mod 4 (within p ≡ 3 (4), which is always ES-easy but count still varies).
first_step: Compute on p ≡ 3 (4) ≤ 2·10⁵: ρ(U, P⁺(p−1)) and mean over safe primes.

title: Primes p with p−1 = 2^k·m, m small: Fermat-like primes as hard cases
connection: Fermat primes 17, 257, 65537 have p ≡ 1 mod 2⁴, 2⁸, 2¹⁶ respectively; compute U(p)/log²p for them: the 2-adic depth effect (−9% per level?) would compound.
why: Direct test of whether 2-adic depth effect saturates (32 vs 16 effect was small) or compounds.
first_step: Run z52b_count on 65537, 257, 17 and on primes 2^k·3+1, 2^k·5+1.

title: Proth-type primes k·2^n + 1 with small k as an ES-hardness test bed
connection: Primes k·2^n+1 (k ≤ 15) have deep 2-adic structure and controllable p−1; scanning U(p)/log² over them separates 2-adic depth from other effects.
why: Large known families (Proth primes) give hard-ish test primes at sizes 10⁶–10¹² where generic censuses are too expensive.
first_step: List Proth primes ≤ 10⁸ and compute R(p), U(p) via targeted solvers.

title: ES hardness index vs class number of Q(ζ_p)^+? (too expensive; proxy via h(p))
connection: Compute-and-check (proxy): cyclotomic class-number data are unavailable at scale; the quadratic subfield Q(√p) (h(p) null) is the only cheap proxy.
why: Records that the cyclotomic-unit / Vandiver-type world shows no signal at the quadratic level.
first_step: Skip unless a specific cyclotomic mechanism is proposed.

title: p mod 5 and p mod 7 as integers are uninformative (|ρ| ≤ 0.07)
connection: Raw residues p mod 5, p mod 7 show tiny correlation; the information is in the Legendre symbols (5/p), (7/p) (and for 7 even that is null).
why: Sanity: ES local dependence is via characters, not the residue's numeric value.
first_step: None.

title: Mordell's identity classes as indicator features: which one explains most variance?
connection: For each classical polynomial identity (mod 3, 5, 7, 8, 11, …) define 1[p in identity class] and regress U(p) on all of them.
why: Identifies the identities that matter for the *count*, not just existence — a 'weighting' of the Mordell covering useful for heuristics.
first_step: Encode Mordell's and Vaughan's identity classes (cf. MODEL_SPECIFIC.md) as features and run a LASSO.

title: Number of distinct x vs number of solutions per x: concentration index
connection: U(p)/nx(p) (solutions per first denominator) is a concentration fingerprint; Gini coefficient of the x-profile per prime.
why: If solutions concentrate on few x, ES at p reduces to few divisor problems — relevant to POINTWISE strategies.
first_step: Compute U/nx at p ≤ 2·10⁵ (both in data) and its dependence on χ_p.

title: Linear-algebra fingerprint: rank of the solution set's denominator matrix mod small primes
connection: For each p, collect (x,y,z) mod q (q = 3, 5, 7) of all solutions; the occupied residue patterns form a fingerprint; compare across hard and easy primes.
why: Local solution patterns at q are exactly what covering congruences use; hard primes should occupy few patterns.
first_step: Compute for p ≤ 10⁴ (needs solution lists — extend the counter to dump solutions).

title: U(p) for p ≡ 3 (4): correlation profile mirrors p ≡ 1 (4)?
connection: All correlations above were computed for p ≡ 1 (4); for p ≡ 3 (4) ES is trivial but counts still fluctuate — compare the χ_p fit.
why: If the same Euler-product law holds, the count law is uniform across classes — a sign it comes from the surface's local densities, not from ES-specific structure.
first_step: Rerun z52b_fingerprint_lfit.py restricted to p ≡ 3 (4).

title: Composite n: is U(n) multiplicative-ish? (U(pq) vs U(p), U(q))
connection: Compute-and-check: for n = pq ≤ 30 000, regress log U(pq) on log U(p), log U(q).
why: ES for composites is inherited from prime factors; quantifying how the count lifts tells whether the 'solution sheaf' is multiplicative.
first_step: Use f4_all_30000.txt; scatter log U(pq) − log U(p) − log U(q).

title: U(p²) and U(p³): prime powers fingerprint
connection: Compute U at prime squares and cubes (in range: p² ≤ 30 000): odd squares kill all certificate lines (T1) but ES(p²) holds via p — how big is U(p²)?
why: T1 says line counts vanish at squares; U(p²) shows how many 'non-line' solutions exist — a measure of what T1-avoiding methods must capture.
first_step: Extract U(m²) for odd m ≤ 173 from the data and compare with U at neighbouring non-squares.

title: Per-prime weights of (q/p) in log U(p): q ≡ 2 (mod 3) give a clean Euler pattern q·β_q ≈ −0.35
connection: Regressing residual log U(p) (p ≡ 1 mod 4, n≈8 400) on (q/p) for q < 80: q·β_q = −0.46, −0.35, −0.37, −0.32, −0.26, −0.38 for q = 5, 11, 17, 23, 29, 47 (≈ constant, as an Euler factor would give), but q ≡ 1 (mod 3) give −0.11, −0.05, −0.17, −0.06, +0.30, +0.26 for q = 7, 13, 19, 31, 37, 43 (SE ≈ 0.002·q); stable across ranges and p mod 3.
why: A sharp, reproducible local-weight fingerprint; any heuristic model of ES counts must reproduce the q mod 3 split.
first_step: Explain via (−3/q) (next item); then refit including indicators 1[q | p+3] to see if the dichotomy disappears.

title: Candidate explanation of the q mod 3 dichotomy: p ≡ −3 (mod q) forces (p/q) = (−3/q)
connection: The strongest single shift is x = (p+3)/4 (ρ(U, τ(p+3)) = +0.48); q | p+3 ⟺ p ≡ −3 (q), which forces (q/p) = (p/q) = (−3/q) = +1 iff q ≡ 1 (mod 3). So for q ≡ 1 (3) 'q is a QR' is positively confounded with 'q divides p+3' (more solutions), cancelling the generic negative QR effect.
why: Candidate mechanism (not yet tested by the controlled regression in the first step): the greedy first step x = ⌈(p+1)/4⌉ couples ES counts to the cubic-residue-flavoured symbol (−3/q). Every first-denominator shift s similarly couples via (−s/q).
first_step: Verify by adding 1[q | p+3] features; then search for the full 'shift ⊗ character' structure: weight of (q/p) ≈ Σ_s w_s·(−s/q)·(…).

title: The '(7/p) anomaly' is plausibly the same (−3/q) confound
connection: Earlier item: U(p) ignores (7/p) (ρ = −0.013); per-prime fit gives 7·β₇ = −0.11 vs ≈ −0.4 for neighbours; 7 ≡ 1 (mod 3) ⇒ (−3/7) = +1 ⇒ confound with 7 | p+3.
why: If confirmed, removes a false lead (no special role of 7 in ES) and illustrates the shift-character coupling.
first_step: Check after controlling for 1[7 | p+3], 1[7 | p+7], … whether β₇ returns to ≈ −0.06.

title: For p ≡ 3 (mod 4) the weights are a clean positive Euler product in χ_{−p}
why: At p ≡ 3 (4) ES is trivial, yet the count law is a textbook Euler product — ES counts are governed by the local densities of the surface; the p ≡ 1 (4) case is the same law with sign flip and shift confounds.
first_step: Derive the local density at q of solutions of 4/p = 1/x+1/y+1/z (Elsholtz–Tao §2-style) as a function of (q/p) and compare to q·β_q ≈ 0.4.

title: Sign flip between p ≡ 1 and p ≡ 3 (mod 4): QR-ness of small primes helps at 3 (mod 4), hurts at 1 (mod 4)
connection: β_q are uniformly positive for p ≡ 3 (4) and mostly negative for p ≡ 1 (4) (for U, k₁, k₂, Uv).
why: At p ≡ 3 (4), (q/p) = χ_{−p}(q) (imaginary field Q(√−p)) and enters positively: U grows with L(1,χ_{−p}) ∝ h(−p)/√p; at p ≡ 1 (4), (q/p) = χ_p(q) (real field Q(√p)) and enters negatively: U shrinks as L(1,χ_p) = 2h(p)log ε_p/√p grows. Imaginary-quadratic L-values help, real-quadratic ones hurt.
first_step: Fit a model U ∝ L(1,χ_{−p})^{a} at p ≡ 3 and L(1,χ_p)^{b} at p ≡ 1 and compare |a|, |b| (≈ 0.4 vs ≈ 0.3?).

title: (★) count R(p): weights β₃ = −0.15, β₇ = −0.08, β₅ = +0.03 (p ≡ 1 mod 4)
connection: R(p)'s per-prime profile differs from U's: dominated by 3 and 7 (both ≡ 3 mod 4) with 5, 17 slightly positive — i.e. R follows (−1/q)(q/p) = χ_{−4p}(q) at q ≡ 1 (4) partially.
why: Pinpoints which local primes the (★) line is sensitive to — a covering argument for (★) should treat 3 and 7 specially.
first_step: Compute the 3-adic and 7-adic local densities of (★) triples (u,B,C) as a function of p mod 3, mod 7.

title: I3 count has β₇ = +0.039 (p ≡ 1 mod 4): QR at 7 helps I3
connection: Unlike U, I3(p) gains when 7 is a QR mod p; k₂ and Uv have β₇ ≈ −0.045.
why: Different certificate families have opposite responses at the same local prime — evidence for complementary families (union arguments) at the level of local densities.
first_step: Tabulate sign(β_q) per family for q ≤ 50 and find pairs of families with opposite sign at many q.

title: Shift spectrum ρ(U, τ(p+s)) is a mod-3 sign pattern
connection: For p ≡ 1 (4): ρ(U-residual, τ(p+s)) > 0 for s ≡ 1 (mod 3) (≈ +0.1…+0.24), < 0 for s ≡ 2 (mod 3) (≈ −0.05…−0.25); s = 3: +0.48 (the genuine first-step effect).
why: Mostly a confound: 3 | p+s identifies p mod 3, and p ≡ 2 (3) is ES-easy. The residual after stratifying by p mod 3 gives the true shift spectrum.
first_step: Recompute ρ within p ≡ 1 (3) and within p ≡ 2 (3) separately.

title: ES count at odd squares is normal: U(m²)/median(neighbours) has median 0.92
connection: For odd m ≤ 173, U(m²) is typical (median ratio 0.92, mean 2.5 because m² with smooth m has huge counts: U(225) = 317, U(441) = 491), although every certificate line vanishes at odd squares (T1).
