why: Certificate lines see none of the solutions at odd squares, yet the total count there is typical — at m² the solutions come from the composite structure (not all are scalings of 4/m solutions: (4, 6, 36) solves 4/9 but is not a scaled solution of 4/3); a proof via lines must route squares through factors.
first_step: Classify the solutions of 4/m² by whether they are scaled solutions of 4/d for some d | m², d < m², and measure the non-inherited fraction.

title: Prime squares p²: what fraction of ES solutions is inherited from 4/p?
connection: Data: U(9) = 6, U(25) = 10, U(49) = 18, U(81) = 46, U(121) = 24, U(169) = 24, U(289) = 27; test for p² ≤ 30 000 whether every solution of 4/p² arises by scaling a solution of 4/p or from the divisor structure of p².
why: Inheritance is not universal ((4, 6, 36) for 4/9 is not a scaled solution of 4/3), so the inherited fraction is a real statistic; if it tends to 1, T1 is 'lines see only primitive solutions'.
first_step: Dump solutions for 4/p² (p ≤ 173) and test inheritance by gcd structure.

title: Composite U(pq) depends weakly on U(p), U(q): log U(pq) ≈ 3.0 + 0.20 log U(p) + 0.11 log U(q) + 0.26 log n
connection: Over 5 668 odd semiprimes pq ≤ 30 000 (p < q), counts at pq are mostly governed by size, mildly by the factors' counts.
why: ES at composites reduces to primes for existence, but counts are 'more than inherited' — composite n have many non-inherited solutions; irrelevant to ES existence but relevant to count heuristics on all n.
first_step: Separate inherited (scaled from 4/p or 4/q) and non-inherited solutions at pq.

title: Easy primes: U(p) records eventually all ≡ −1 (mod 840)
why: Mirror of the hard primes (≡ 1 mod 840): ES-easiest primes are ≡ −1 modulo highly composite numbers (5039 = 7! − 1 = 2·2520 − 1). The count is a function of p's position relative to smooth numbers.
first_step: Note 55439 = 2·27720 − 1 and 5039 = 2·2520 − 1 are records; test the next candidates 2·lcm(1..k) − 1 and lcm(1..k) − 1 when prime; OEIS search of the record list gave no match.

title: Symmetry p ↔ −p modulo smooth moduli: hard at 1 (mod L), easy at −1 (mod L)
connection: Hard primes cluster at p ≡ 1 (mod 840), record-easy primes at p ≡ −1 (mod 840).
why: ES identities exist for p ≡ −a (mod b) classes (n ≡ −1 mod 4 trivially, etc.), so p ≡ −1 mod L hits all identity classes with a=1 — the residue −1 is 'universally covered', +1 'universally uncovered'. A clean formulation of the covering obstruction.
first_step: Count for each modulus L | 840 how many classical identity classes contain −1 and +1 (mod L).

title: Proth primes are not hard: 65537 (ratio 0.96), 786433 (0.92), 5767169 (1.44), 104857601 (1.62)
connection: Deep 2-adic structure alone (p ≡ 1 mod 2^k) does not make ES hard; 193 = 3·2⁶+1 (0.22), 97 (0.38), 769 (0.41) moderately hard at small size.
why: Separates 2-adic depth from the full smooth-p−1 profile; ES hardness needs many small primes simultaneously ≡ 1-ish, not one deep prime power.
first_step: Regress U(p)/log² on v₂(p−1), v₃(p−1), v₅(p−1) jointly with the χ_p Euler product to apportion.

title: 2-adic depth effect saturates at 16
why: The 2-adic local density of ES solutions seems to depend on p mod 16 only — a finite local datum, consistent with the 'four-adic input' picture (FOUR_ADIC_INPUT.md).
first_step: Compute the exact 2-adic density of the ES surface at p mod 64 by counting solutions mod 2^k.

title: Reversal: does the count law predict which numbers m/p fail (Schinzel)?
connection: Use the fitted ES-count Euler product with numerator-m analogue to predict log U_m(p); compare predicted lowest values with actual failures m ∈ [8, 48].
why: A successful prediction would show the Schinzel failures are exactly 'local-density-small' primes — supporting PW's probabilistic picture with arithmetic content.
first_step: Fit per-q weights for each m (data on disk) and compute AUC of predicted log U_m for failure vs non-failure.

title: Binary expansion of hard primes: no signal expected (null test)
connection: Hamming weight / trailing-ones of p in binary for the 40 hardest vs random p ≡ 1 (24): any difference beyond v₂(p−1) would be surprising.
why: Sanity test of the 'digits are irrelevant' prior; only v₂(p−1) (trailing zeros of p−1) is arithmetic.
first_step: Compute and record; expect null after conditioning on v₂(p−1).

title: Continued fraction of 4/p and its partial quotients vs U(p)
connection: 4/p has a short CF; ES₅ ⟺ λ(p) ≤ 3 is about CF lengths of p/A for certain A. Correlate U(p) with the CF length/max partial quotient of p/A over small A.
why: Bridges the CF formulation (Zaremba-type, ZAREMBA_TRANSFER.md) to the count; a strong correlation would suggest Zaremba/Bourgain–Kontorovich density tools apply.
first_step: For each p compute #{A < p : CF length of p/A ≤ 3} (the five-slice count) and Spearman with U(p).

title: Five-slice count ES₅(p) vs U(p): fraction of solutions with λ ≤ 3
connection: FRONTIER notes 56% of solutions below 3000 lie outside the five-slice family; fingerprint the fraction per prime and its dependence on χ_p.
why: If the five-slice fraction is stable and bounded below, ES₅ is 'ES with a constant loss' empirically, supporting ES ⇒ ES₅.
first_step: Implement the λ(p) ≤ 3 certificate counter (HJ-length of p/A) and compute ratio at p ≤ 10⁵.

title: Hirzebruch–Jung length fingerprint of hard primes
connection: λ(p) (minimal HJ/CF length certificate) for hard primes vs random: are hard primes the ones with λ(p) = 3 exactly (no length-2 certificates)?
why: λ(p) is a discrete hardness grade; its distribution conditional on χ_p would connect CF dynamics with the Euler-product count law.
first_step: Compute λ(p) for p ≤ 10⁵ (existing scripts? check scripts/*hj*) and cross-tabulate with U(p)/log² quantiles.

title: k₁/k₂ ratio as a function of p mod 24
connection: Type I : Type II proportions at primes differ by p mod 8 and mod 3 (via the characters above); the ratio fingerprint may reveal which type 'rescues' the hard classes.
why: If for p ≡ 1 (24) Type II dominates, Type II is the natural attack for the hard class.
first_step: Tabulate mean k₁/(k₁+k₂) by p mod 24 and by p mod 840 square classes.

title: Hard-prime 'deficit vectors' over local primes
connection: For each hard prime compute the vector ((q/p))_{q≤47} and 1[q | p+3], 1[q | p−1]; cluster hard primes by these vectors.
why: If hard primes form a few clusters (e.g. 'all small q QR' and 'p−1 smooth'), each cluster may need a different certificate family.
first_step: k-means on the 200 hardest primes ≤ 2·10⁵ with these binary features.

title: Predicting R-zeros from local data: AUC test
connection: Train logistic regression on (q/p), 1[q | 4Cp+1] for small q, C to predict R(p) ≤ 2 (near-zeros) at p ≤ 3·10⁶; evaluate on the 12 zeros.
why: High AUC would show (★) failures are locally predictable — consistent with 'failures are discrete local events' and suggesting a finite covering-by-local-conditions proof might handle all but a predictable sparse set.
first_step: Build features for p ≡ 1 (4) ≤ 3·10⁶; R from words_3e6.npy.

title: Least C with a (★) certificate vs p mod small numbers
connection: Cmin(p) (least C with a divisor d | 4Cp+1, d ≡ −1 (4C)) should depend on p mod 3, 5, 7 via which C make 4Cp+1 divisible by small primes.
why: A table of E[Cmin | p mod 840] is a direct, computable covering-cost fingerprint.
first_step: Compute Cmin for p ≤ 10⁶ and average by p mod 840.

title: Carmichael numbers are ES-rich, not ES-hard: U(n) is 3.3–5.7× the neighbour median
why: Although n ≡ 1 modulo each p−1 (the 'hard' congruence shape), having ≥ 3 prime factors multiplies divisor structure; the p ≡ 1 (mod L) hardness mechanism does not survive multiplicatively — hardness is a prime phenomenon.
first_step: Compare with semiprimes pq where both p, q are ES-hard (e.g. 193·241) to see whether hardness compounds at all.

title: Pairwise union conjecture: (★) ∪ U covers every non-square n ≡ 1 (4) ≤ 3·10⁶ except 105
connection: Joint zeros of R and Uv among non-square n ≡ 1 (mod 4), n ≤ 3·10⁶: only {105}. Same for R ∩ I3 = {105} and Uv ∩ I3 = {105}.
why: Any two of the three word families jointly certify ES on all non-square n ≡ 1 (4) in range (squares are T1-dead for all lines). A two-family statement is the most economical union target and stronger than FRONTIER's (★) ∪ b=1 at primes.
first_step: Extend the joint census to 10⁹ with the segmented sieve; try to find the local reason the families' failure sets are disjoint (different shift/character profiles, cf. per-prime weights).

title: Bounded U-certificate size: Vmin(p) ≤ 116 for all primes p ≡ 1 (4) ≤ 3·10⁶
connection: Least v ∈ 4ℤ ∪ (8ℤ−p), v ≥ 3, with p+v having a divisor ≡ −1 (mod v): records 3 (5), 4 (17), 7 (97), 8 (457), 23 (1009), 87 (2521), 116 (3361) and no further record up to 3·10⁶; 99.9% quantile 31, mean 4.0.
why: A bounded-v version of U ('U_V: some v ≤ V works') is a finite union of single-shift divisor problems; if true for V = 116 it reduces ES at primes to finitely many 'p + v has a divisor ≡ −1 (mod v)' events — exactly the shape where single-shift laws (EXSET_SHIFT_DIVISORS Thm 2.2) apply, though the joint failure probability must still be bounded.
first_step: Extend the Vmin census to 10⁹ at primes; check whether records resume (each single-shift failure has probability ≍ (log p)^{−1/2}, so a fixed finite V must eventually fail infinitely often under independence — the data test that heuristic).

title: Independence heuristic predicts unbounded Vmin; data show a plateau at 116 — test it
connection: If fail_v events at a prime were independent with P(fail_v) ≍ C_v(log p)^{−1/2}, the probability that all v ≤ 116 fail is tiny but the number of primes is huge; compute the expected number of primes ≤ X with Vmin > 116 under the model and compare with 0 observed.
why: A discrepancy would quantify positive dependence/repulsion between shifts (FRONTIER's joint-failure discussion) using a sharp observable.
first_step: Use the single-shift law constants from EXSET_SHIFT_DIVISORS §2 to compute E#{p ≤ 3·10⁶ : Vmin(p) > V} for V = 31, 87, 116.

title: (★) certificate size Cmin: records 1,2,5,20,23,39,40,141,149,251,557 then 23105 at p = 184837
connection: Least C with a (★) word at primes p ≡ 1 (4) ≤ 3·10⁶: mean 1.94, 99% quantile 9, 99.9% 41; the record jump to 23105 at 184837 is a boundary solution (u = 1, B = 2: 4C−1 = (p+1)/2), i.e. 184837 is an 'almost R-zero'.
why: Boundary-only primes (only u=1 or B=1 certificates) behave like R-zeros for any argument that excludes boundary terms; they enlarge the hard set for interior-only methods.
first_step: List all primes ≤ 3·10⁶ whose (★) words are boundary-only; compare their arithmetic profile with the R-zeros.

title: Boundary-only (★) primes as a second hardness list
connection: Compute-and-check: primes p ≡ 1 (4) where every (★) triple has u = 1 or B = 1 (trivial divisor of 4Cp+1 near the boundary); expect them to contain 184837 and be ~10× more numerous than R-zeros.
why: FRONTIER counts R(p) including boundary; interior counts are what equidistribution arguments control — so the interior-zero list is the real target of such arguments.
first_step: Modify the word sieve to count interior (★) words (u, B ≥ 2) and list zeros at primes ≤ 3·10⁶.

title: I3 needs large coordinates: min over I3 words of max(t,u,v) has median 169 and grows (740 at 2.5·10⁶)
connection: At primes p ≡ 1 (4) ≤ 3·10⁶ the smallest I3 certificate has max coordinate ≈ 175 on average, records 379 (487 381) … 740 (2 506 373).
why: I3 is cheap in count but expensive in size — unlike U and (★) (bounded small certificates); an existence proof for I3 can't use small-coordinate coverings.
first_step: Fit the record growth (≈ p^{0.3}?) and relate to the t,u,v ≥ 3 constraint geometry.

title: Mean (★) certificate size ≈ 2 and U size ≈ 4: most primes are certified by C ∈ {1,2}
connection: Cmin(p) = 1 for 76.6% of primes ≡ 1 (4) with a certificate and ≤ 2 for 91.8% (reviewer rerun): i.e. 4p+1 has a divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4), or 8p+1 one ≡ −1 (mod 8), for ≈ 92% of primes.
why: The (★) problem is mostly 'one or two shifted integers have a divisor in a class' — quantitative law: P(Cmin > c) decays fast; the tail (c ≥ 10) contains all hardness.
first_step: Fit P(Cmin > c) for c ≤ 50 and compare with the product of single-event failure probabilities ∏_{C≤c} P(4Cp+1 has no divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C).

title: Tail law of Cmin vs independent divisor events
connection: If the slice failures F_C = {4Cp+1 has no divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4C)} were independent, P(Cmin > c) ≈ ∏_{C≤c} P(F_C), where each P(F_C) decays slowly with p (a single-shift failure law, cf. EXSET_SHIFT_DIVISORS Thm 2.2); compare with data. Also compute the full correlation matrix of the events E_C = ¬F_C for C ≤ 20–32 (φ-coefficients; E_C and E_{2C} share structure).
why: Measures dependence between (★) slices C — exactly the 'joint budget' question (JOINT_BUDGET.md) in a cheap observable.
first_step: Compute empirical P(E_C) and P(E_C ∩ E_C′) at p ≤ 3·10⁶ for C, C′ ≤ 20; report the correlation matrix.

title: 105 is the unique non-square n ≡ 1 (4) ≤ 3·10⁶ killing all three word families
connection: R(105) = Uv(105) = I3(105) = 0 and ESC(105) = 0; every other non-square n ≡ 1 (4) has at least two families alive.
why: 105 = 3·5·7 is 'locally square' modulo 8 and small primes? (105 ≡ 1 mod 8, 105 ≡ 0 mod 3,5,7) — its divisibility by 3,5,7 kills shifts; a structural characterisation would explain uniqueness.
first_step: Check whether n = 3·5·7·m² or other 'n ≡ 0 mod 105' families have systematically few words.

title: U failures factor as products of small primes ≡ 3 (mod 4) and one larger factor
why: Composite U failures are driven by the composite structure (factors ≡ 3 mod 4 make n+v divisors in the needed class scarce?); 25305 contains 241 (least p ≡ 1 (4) with least QNR 7) — a weak link to pseudosquare-type hardness.
first_step: Test whether U-failure rate among n ≡ 1 (8) depends on the number of prime factors ≡ 3 (mod 4) of n; predict further failures beyond 10⁹ from that profile.

title: Normal-form lemma (proved): in every solution x ≤ y ≤ z of 4/p (p odd prime), p divides z
connection: Proof: x ≤ 3p/4 < p so p ∤ x; reducing mod p forces p | y or p | z. Suppose p ∤ z, y = pb: then (4b−1)xz = pb(x+z) so 4b−1 = pt; with a = 4x−p > 0 one gets z = pbx/(ab−x), and z ≥ pb gives x < ab ≤ 2x, hence t ≤ 1/p + 2/a; a ≥ 3 is impossible for odd p, and a = 1 forces t = 1, b = x, contradicting ab > x (proof completed by the review subagent). Data: all 21 909 solutions for p < 2500 checked directly; share check at all primes ≤ 10⁵.
why: Explains minz(p) ≡ 0 (mod p) and gives a normal form ('z-anchored') for all ES solutions at primes — useful for parametrisations; it says nothing about existence.
first_step: Record as a lemma; check it is ET's Type I/II dichotomy in disguise (k₁ ↔ only z divisible, k₂ ↔ y, z divisible).

title: Isosceles solutions (two equal denominators) exist at a prime iff p ≡ 3 (mod 4) (or p = 2)
connection: The primes ≤ 10⁵ with no solution having x = y or y = z are exactly the 4 783 primes ≡ 1 (mod 4) (OEIS first-20 match: A002144 Pythagorean primes); composite failures ≤ 3000 start 25, 65, 85, … (all prime factors ≡ 1 mod 4?).
why: A clean exact statement linking ES degenerate solutions to sums of two squares; the obstruction for p ≡ 1 (4) in the degenerate locus is exactly the hard class — a 'degenerate T1'.
first_step: Prove: 4/p = 2/x + 1/z or 1/x + 2/z solvable ⟺ p ≢ 1 (4) (reduce to a two-term problem 4/p − 2/x = 1/z, a divisor-in-class condition, show it needs a divisor ≡ 3 (mod 4) of something like p²); check composite failure set = n with all prime factors ≡ 1 (4) (A004613).

title: 'lcm-closed' solutions (x | z): fail only at 2521 among all primes ≤ 10⁵ and all n ≤ 3000
connection: Solutions with x | z (equivalently y | z in the data: identical failure set and share 0.377) exist for every prime ≤ 10⁵ except 2521 = lcm(1..10)+1, the hardest ES prime; none of the 9 solutions of 4/2521 has x | z.
why: A sub-family with a single exception ≤ 10⁵ — and the exception is the extremal 'all small primes split' prime. 4/p = (a + b + 1)/z with a, b | z is a pure 'three divisors of z summing to 4z/p' problem: a practical-number style formulation.
first_step: Extend to 10⁷; test whether failures are exactly primes ≡ 1 (mod lcm(1..k)) with k large; prove x | z ⟺ y | z for prime n.

title: x | z ⟺ y | z for every solution at a prime (proved from the normal form)
connection: Since p | z, 4z/p = z/x + z/y + 1 is an integer identity: if x | z then z/y is an integer, and conversely. Data agree (identical failure sets and share 0.377).
why: Suggests a structural lemma: at a prime, x | z forces y | z (and conversely), i.e. z = lcm(x, y) — a rigid sub-family amenable to a parametrisation by divisors of z/p.
first_step: Use the lcm-closed family z = lcm(x, y) as a parametrisation by divisors of z/p (three divisors a, b of z with a + b + 1 = 4z/p).

title: Divisor-chain x | y never fails (all primes ≤ 10⁵, all n ≤ 3000)
connection: Every n in range has an ES solution with x | y (share 0.14 of solutions); 4/n − 1/z = (k+1)/(kx) means 4/n − 1/z = a/b (lowest terms) with b having a divisor ≡ −1 (mod a).
why: x | y is the 'divisor ≡ −1 (mod a)' event again — equivalent in spirit to the word families (tuv − u − v); a direct bridge between the Egyptian-fraction shape and the word/U formulation.
first_step: Write the bijection between x | y solutions and words n = tuv − u − v (or a sub-family) and compare counts.

title: Full chain x | y | z fails at 670 primes ≤ 10⁵, starting 73, 193, 313, 337, 409, 457, 577, …
connection: Chains exist for most primes but fail at a sizeable set containing the hard primes 193, 409, 577, 1201 (not in OEIS).
why: The chain sub-family is a 1-parameter-poorer certificate; its failure set is a hardness filter between the full ES and single lines.
first_step: Compute the density of chain failures among p ≡ 1 (24) vs others; is it ≈ constant (then infinitely many failures) or decaying?

title: All-squarefree solutions: fail only at 71, 191, 21 169 among primes ≤ 10⁵
connection: Every prime ≤ 10⁵ except 71, 191, 21169 has an ES solution with x, y, z all squarefree (share 0.15); x squarefree alone never fails (all n ≤ 3000 too).
why: Squarefree denominators are the natural setting for local-global arguments (no prime-power local conditions); a three-exception family is a candidate 'squarefree ES' conjecture. 71 and 191 ≡ 3 (mod 4)!
first_step: Explain 71 and 191 (≡ 7 mod 8, easy for ES but every solution has a square factor); extend census to 10⁷.

title: No-3 solutions (3 ∤ xyz) fail only at 3 and 241
connection: Every prime ≤ 10⁵ except 3 and 241 has an ES solution with none of x, y, z divisible by 3; all 8 solutions of 4/241 contain a multiple of 3. Analogous 'none divisible by 5' fails only at 5, 'by 7' only at 7; 'none divisible by 9 / 8 / 4' never fail at primes.
why: 241 (least p ≡ 1 (4) with least QNR 7, a pseudosquare) is the unique non-trivial obstruction for avoiding 3 — a single-prime 3-adic obstruction.
first_step: Characterise why 241 forces 3 | xyz (check its solutions mod 3: all have x or y,z ≡ 0); search 'no 3' failures to 10⁷.

title: 'Some denominator divisible by 4' fails only at 2, 17, 241
connection: Every prime ≤ 10⁵ except 2, 17, 241 has an ES solution with 4 | x, y or z (share 0.70); 241 again.
why: 241 is simultaneously the last 8/p failure, the last '4 | some denominator' failure and the unique non-trivial 'no 3' failure — a triple 2-/3-adic outlier worth a case study.
first_step: Case study of 4/241: list its 8 solutions (all have a multiple of 3, none a multiple of 4) and relate to 241 ≡ 1 (mod 240).

title: 241 = 240 + 1 as a universal small outlier
connection: 241 appears in: 8/p failures (last), 16/p and 20/p failures (not 12/p), '4 | some denominator' failures (last), 'no 3' failures (unique), U-hard top 30, greedy x = (p+3)/4 failures, z ≤ p^{1.75} failures (first).
why: p − 1 = 240 = 2⁴·3·5 — 241 ≡ 1 (mod 16, 3, 5) is the smallest prime with simultaneous deep 2-adic and 3,5 structure; a natural test case for every new certificate family.
first_step: Add 241, 2521, 193 to every new family's unit tests; record which families certify them.

title: Height: every prime ≤ 10⁵ has a solution with z ≤ p², but 50 primes need z > p^{1.75}
connection: z ≤ p² never fails; z ≤ p^{1.75} fails at 50 primes (241, 269, 367, 449, 577, 601, …, last 95327); z ≤ p^{1.5} fails at 7 109 primes.
why: A height-bounded ES ('z ≤ p²') is a finite search per prime with a clean conjectural exponent between 1.75 and 2 — the right scale for effective/lattice approaches (LATTICE_MEETING.md).
first_step: Compute max_{p≤X} log(minz(p))/log p up to 10⁷ and check whether it tends to 2 from below.

title: Primitive solutions (gcd(x,y,z) = 1) fail at 110 primes ≤ 10⁵, all ≡ 1 (mod 12)
connection: No primitive ES solution at 13, 37, 97, 181, 193, 277, 373, 541, 673, 757, 853, 1033, 1093, 1297, 1621, … (last ≤ 10⁵: 98713); share of primitive solutions 7.9%.
why: Primitive points on the ES cubic surface are the integral-point problem proper; failures concentrated on p ≡ 1 (12) show the 3-adic and 4-adic local structure of primitivity.
first_step: Check that all 110 are ≡ 1 (mod 12) and compute failure density in that class (≈ 110/1200?); likely infinite — record as 'primitive ES fails infinitely often?' question.

title: Coprime-pair solutions fail at 1 285 primes (13, 37, 61, 97, 109, 181, 193, …)
connection: Solutions with gcd(x,y) = 1 (equivalently some coprime pair, identical failure set) are absent at 1 285 primes ≤ 10⁵, all apparently ≡ 1 (mod 12).
why: Pairwise-coprime structure fails generically on p ≡ 1 (12): every ES solution there shares factors — consistent with the 'multiplicative' Type I/II constructions.
first_step: Verify the mod-12 claim and compute the failure density in p ≡ 1 (12).

title: At odd n, every solution has at least two even denominators
connection: Exactly-0-even and exactly-1-even solutions never occur at primes (2-adic parity: three odd unit fractions sum to odd/odd; one even denominator gives odd numerator over even); shares: 2 even 52%, all even 48%.
why: Trivial 2-adic lemma but a useful normal form: write x = 2x₁ or the pair y, z even; reduces 2-adic case analysis in parametrisations.
first_step: None beyond writing down the lemma.

title: Solutions with x prime fail at 4 597 primes; with some perfect-square denominator at 3 134
connection: Prime smallest denominators (share 0.7%) and square denominators (0.8%) are rare; failure sets start 31, 37, 53, 73, … and 17, 29, 41, 73, 89, … (no OEIS match).
why: Rare-shape sub-families give no ES leverage but are fingerprints for 'random-like' behaviour of denominators (density of primes/squares among x).
first_step: Compare the share of prime x with 1/log x heuristics (≈ 1/log(p/4)).

title: Power-of-2 denominators are rare (fail at 9 483 of 9 592 primes)
connection: Only ≈ 1.1% (109) of primes ≤ 10⁵ have a solution with a power of 2 among x, y, z (TWO_POWER_LADDER.md studies such ladders).
why: Calibration for any approach via 2-power denominators: it can certify only a thin set of primes.
first_step: List primes with a 2-power solution and compare with the ladder families in TWO_POWER_LADDER.md.

title: Shares of solution shapes at primes ≈ constants: x | z 0.377, none-div-by-3 0.346, none-div-by-4 0.301, none-div-by-8 0.59, none-div-by-9 0.70
connection: Mean share (over p ≡ 1 (4) > 1000) of each restricted shape among all solutions; these are local-density-like constants of the ES solution set.
why: Stable shares across p would mean the solution set equidistributes in these local conditions (Manin-type equidistribution on the surface) — compare with local densities computed mod 3, 4, 8, 9.
first_step: Compute shares per dyadic range to see whether they converge; compute the local densities predicted by counting solutions mod q.

title: Composite failures for 'none of x, y, z divisible by 4': exactly multiples of 16
connection: Among n ≤ 3000 the n with no ES solution having 4 ∤ x, 4 ∤ y, 4 ∤ z are 16, 32, 48, …; the analogous condition for 8 fails exactly at multiples of 32, for 9 at multiples of 9, for 5 at multiples of 5.
why: Clean local lemmas (p-adic valuation of n forces valuations of denominators); sanity checks for the variant engine.
first_step: Prove: v₂(n) ≥ 4 ⇒ 4 | some denominator; v₃(n) ≥ 2 ⇒ 9 | some denominator.

title: 'Only z divisible by n' fails at all powers of 2 (composites ≤ 3000)
connection: At n = 2^k every solution has ≥ 2 denominators divisible by n (or none); at odd primes the k₁-shape always exists.
why: Powers of 2 are the ES 'easy' case but structurally degenerate; sanity fingerprint for the normal-form lemma.
first_step: None.

title: Restricted-ES variant failure sets are mostly NOT in OEIS
connection: Lookups of the failure sets (chain, primitive, coprime-pair, squarefree, height p^{1.75}, prime-x, square-denominator) returned no OEIS match; only the isosceles set matched (A002144).
why: A family of ~10 new, cheaply-defined sequences: submitting them invites outside pattern-matching (e.g. someone may recognise the primitive-failure primes).
first_step: Bundle and submit with definitions, after verifying with an independent brute-force for p ≤ 2000.

title: Union of restricted families: smallest set of shapes covering all primes
connection: Shapes with tiny failure sets ≤ 10⁵: lcm-closed {2521}; all-squarefree {71, 191, 21169}; none-div-by-3 {3, 241}; some-denominator-div-by-4 {2, 17, 241}. lcm-closed ∪ none-div-by-3 covers every prime ≤ 10⁵ (lcm-closed certifies 3). Not all pairs are disjoint: none-div-by-3 and 4-divides-some both fail at 241.
why: Each shape has its own local structure; a proof of 'every p has an lcm-closed or 3-free solution' might be easier than ES if the two obstructions are incompatible (2521 vs 241 are different local profiles).
first_step: Find the local reason for each single exception and test whether any prime can fail two shapes simultaneously (search to 10⁷).

title: Case study 4/2521: no solution has x | z, all have small x ∈ [636, 1026]
connection: The 9 solutions of 4/2521 have x ∈ {636, 638, 644, 652, 658, 748, 1026}, none with x | z; residues mod 3 and mod 4 are mixed.
why: 2521 is the unique lcm-closed failure and the hardest prime ≤ 2·10⁵ by U/log²p; understanding its 9 solutions (5 have 4 | x) is a concrete testbed for 'why is p ≡ 1 (mod 2520) hard'.
first_step: For each solution identify its ET type and the (★)/U/I3 word that generates it; compute what fails for the lcm-closed family (which divisor sums 4z/p = a + b + 1 are missing).

title: Primitive-failure primes vs R-zeros and Type-A failures
connection: 193 is a primitive failure; check overlap of the 110 primitive failures with the hard lists (R-zeros 409, 577, 5569, 9601, 23929, 83449 are p ≡ 1 (24); some are ≡ 1 (12)).
why: If primitive failures and line failures overlap strongly, the lines are 'primitive-solution detectors'.
first_step: Intersect the sets (variants.json) and compute the hypergeometric p-value.

title: Variant engine for m/n: restricted shapes for 5/n and 8/n
connection: Rerun the variant counters for numerators 5 and 8 (one flag) to get Sierpiński / even-ES analogues of the isosceles, lcm-closed and primitive fingerprints.
why: If '4/p isosceles ⟺ p ≡ 3 (4)' has a clean 5/p analogue (p in a class mod 5 or 20?) it reveals the general degenerate-locus law.
first_step: Run z52b_fingerprint_variants with m = 5, 8 on primes ≤ 10⁵.

title: The χ_p correlation persists out of sample at 10⁶ and 10⁷
connection: Spearman(U(p), log L₃₁(1,χ_p)) = −0.62 (156 primes ≡ 1 (4) in [10⁶, 10⁶+4000]) and −0.69 (113 primes in [10⁷, 10⁷+4000]); k₁ −0.66/−0.75, k₂ −0.38/−0.36 — same strength as at ≤ 2·10⁵ (rank correlations; the fitted exponent α ≈ −0.30 itself was not re-estimated).
why: The correlation is scale-stable, so the χ_p dependence is not small-number noise; whether the exponent is stable needs the refit in the first step.
first_step: Push to 10⁹ windows (count program ≈ 100 s per prime there) and track whether the exponent α ≈ −0.3 drifts.

title: U(232 792 561) = 276: the lcm(1..19)+1 prime is hard but not extreme
connection: p = lcm(1,…,19)+1 has U = 276, U/log²p = 0.74, U/log³p = 0.039 vs median U/log³p ≈ 0.095 at 10⁷ (below the minimum of 113 random primes at 10⁷); k₁ = 193, k₂ = 83 (k₁/k₂ = 2.3, typical). [An earlier version reported k₁ = 47 < k₂ = 82 — an artefact of a 64-bit overflow in the type classification, fixed after review.]
why: Partially confirms the lcm+1 prediction (hard, ≈ 2.5× below typical) but not 'record-hard'; the Type I/II split is normal, so all-small-primes-split does not starve Type I specifically at this prime.
first_step: Model-guided search for primes ≡ 1 (mod 2520·11·13) ≤ 10¹⁰ with extreme L(1,χ_p); compare their U/log³p with the lcm(1..19)+1 value.

title: Does the Type I share fall with L(1,χ_p)? (k₁ responds more strongly than k₂)
connection: Across p ≤ 2·10⁵, k₁ has α ≈ −0.34 on log L(1,χ_p), k₂ only ≈ −0.20, so the Type I share k₁/(k₁+k₂) should decrease as L(1,χ_p) grows; at lcm(1..19)+1 the split is nevertheless typical (k₁/k₂ = 2.3).
why: If the share effect were strong, a proof strategy could split by the size of L(1,χ_p) (Type I when some small prime is inert, Type II otherwise); the residual k₁/k₂ correlation +0.70 and the lcm(1..19)+1 data suggest the effect is modest.
first_step: Fit k₁/(k₁+k₂) against log L(1,χ_p) at p ≤ 10⁷ windows and at pseudosquare primes.

title: Rédei 4-/8-rank of Cl(−4p) has no effect (h(−4p) mod 16 strata differ by ≤ 0.016 in residual log counts)
connection: For p ≡ 1 (8), residual log U, k₁, k₂, R by h(−4p) mod 16 ∈ {0,4,8,12}: |differences| ≤ 0.016.
why: Another higher-character null: 8-rank (Barrucand–Cohn: p = x²+32y²) governs quartic/octic symbols, which the data already showed are irrelevant.
first_step: None; record.

title: Median U(p)/log²p rises 1.33 → 1.54 from 10⁶ to 10⁷ (log³ growth)
connection: Window medians (p ≡ 1 (4)): 1.33 at 10⁶, 1.54 at 10⁷; minimum 0.61 (10⁶) and 0.88 (10⁷).
why: Consistent with ET's log³ average; the lower envelope also rises — supports 'every prime has ≫ log²p solutions' at least empirically.
first_step: Compare min_{window} U(p)/log³p across windows; if flat, the conjectural lower bound U(p) ≫ log³p / (something) is the right target.

title: Lower envelope of U(p): extreme-value fit
connection: The minimum of U(p)/log³p over windows of N primes should behave like an extreme value of the (approximately lognormal) residual — Gumbel scaling predicts min ≈ median·exp(−σ√(2 log N)).
why: If minima fall faster than Gumbel, there are arithmetic 'hard families' (e.g. lcm+1) beyond the bulk; slower ⇒ bulk-dominated. Distinguishes the two pictures of ES hardness.
first_step: Estimate σ of residual log U at 10⁶/10⁷ (≈ 0.25?) and compare predicted vs observed window minima and the 2·10⁵ global minimum (2521).

title: Targeted search for record-hard primes via the fitted model
connection: Rank candidate primes p ≡ 1 (mod 840) up to 10¹² by predicted log U (Euler product over q ≤ 50 + 2-adic depth + τ((p+3)/4)) and compute U only for the top predictions.
why: Finds the hardest ES primes at scales where exhaustive counting is impossible — the best stress-test inputs for any proposed certificate family.
first_step: Implement: sieve p ≡ 1 (840) with all q ≤ 23 QR, then rank by τ((p+3)/4) and v₂(p−1); count U at the top 100 in [10⁹, 10¹⁰].

title: Does any prime > 2·10⁵ beat 2521's U/log³p?
why: If 2521 stays the global minimum of U/log³p, ES hardness is bounded below in normalised form — a strong empirical lower bound U(p) ≥ 0.019 log³p.
first_step: Model-guided search (previous item) for p ≤ 10¹⁰ with U/log³p < 0.03.

title: The (★) mean constant vs BM mean: R/M_BM ≈ 1.31 (p ≤ 12 000) and 1.22 (20 000–30 000)
connection: Mean ratio of R(p) to the BM main term drifts down with p (M₀ ratio 1.26 → 1.18).
why: If R/M_BM → 1 the BM term is asymptotically the right mean (FRONTIER: M_BM ∼ M₀ under GRH); the drift rate measures the secondary term.
first_step: Compute R/M_BM at windows 10⁵, 10⁶, 3·10⁶ (script scales linearly per prime).

title: BM residual correlation with U persists at 20 000–30 000: +0.58
connection: Residual Spearman(M_BM, U) = 0.65 (≤ 12 000) and 0.58 (20 000–30 000); with R only 0.10 / 0.10.
why: Robust: the campaign's BM main term is a strong predictor of the *total* ES count but not of its own (★) count fluctuations — suggests reorganising the BM analysis around U(p) or ESC(p).
first_step: Recompute the BM-type main term for the ESC family (all coordinates) and check whether it predicts ESC(p) fluctuations.

title: F_q-point counts of the ES surface do not depend on p mod q — unrestricted point counts do not explain the (q/p) dependence of solution counts
connection: For q ≤ 47, #{4xyz = p(xy+yz+zx)} over F_q is q²+1 (affine) and q²−3q+3 on the torus xyz ≠ 0, identical for every p ≢ 0 (mod q) (scaling x,y,z by p is an isomorphism; same for the Type I/II parametrisations).
why: Unrestricted F_q point counts (hence the naive singular series) cannot explain the Euler-product-shaped dependence of U(p) on (q/p); a Brauer-restricted / Hilbert-symbol counting mechanism (Bright–Loughran's BM class, the campaign's M_BM = M₀ − T(p)) is a candidate explanation — not established by this experiment.
first_step: Derive the expected count of Type I/II solutions including the quadratic-character term from the Brauer element and compare its predicted per-prime weights with the fitted β_q ≈ −0.35/q.

title: Predict per-prime weights β_q from the BM main term
connection: M_BM(p) = Σ (1 − (−uB/p))/φ(4uB): expanding (−uB/p) = ∏_{q|uB} (q/p)^{v_q} predicts how each (q/p) shifts the mean count; compare with q·β_q ≈ −0.35 for q ≡ 2 (3) and the q ≡ 1 (3) confound.
why: A quantitative match would show the BM term is the full explanation of the χ_p fluctuations of U; a mismatch identifies missing terms (e.g. the shift couplings via (−s/q)).
first_step: Compute ∂ E[M_BM | (q/p) = ±1] numerically at p ≤ 30 000 for each q ≤ 47 and plot against fitted β_q.

title: Markov primes vs 12/p failures: {2, 5, 13, 29, 433} = Markov ∩ fail(12) ≤ 10⁵
connection: Markov primes ≤ 10⁵: 2,5,13,29,89,233,433,1597,2897,5741,7561,28657,33461,43261,96557; five lie in the 22-element 12/p failure set (and the same five in fail(24)); 433 is the notable one.
why: Probably small-number coincidence, but Markov numbers m have −1 and other small quantities as QRs mod m (m | a²+b² with structured a, b) — a quadratic-residue profile like ES-hard primes; MARKOFF_ES.md explores Markov ↔ ES.
first_step: Compute the least QNR / L(1,χ_m) quantile for Markov primes and test enrichment in all m/p failure sets with a permutation test.

title: Pell numerology: R-zeros 409 = 408 + 1 and 577 with 577² − 2·408² = 1
connection: The first two (★) failures are 408+1 and 577, the Pell pair (577, 408) for √2; 577 − 1 = 24².
why: Almost certainly coincidence; recorded because √2-convergents p/q give p ≡ ±1 structure and 2 is a QR mod both — test cheaply with the next Pell pairs (3363, 2378), (19601, 13860).
first_step: Check R(p) at primes near Pell numbers (2379, 3361? 3363 is composite; 13861, 19601 composite) — expect nothing.

title: Primes of the form m² + 1 (Landau) as an ES-hardness family
connection: p = m² + 1 has p − 1 a square (τ(p−1) odd) and p ≡ 1 (4); 577 = 24² + 1 is an R-zero. Compute mean residual log U over p = m²+1 ≤ 2·10⁵ vs all p ≡ 1 (4).
why: A polynomial family where p−1 has structured divisors: tests whether 'p−1 has many square factors' matters beyond τ(p−1).
first_step: Run after the data refresh (misc script); report mean residual and the R-zero count among m²+1 primes ≤ 3·10⁶.

title: Function-field analogue of 2521: polynomials ≡ 1 modulo all small irreducibles
connection: Over F_q[T], the analogue of lcm(1..k)+1 is P = ∏_{deg ≤ d} (irreducibles) + 1 (or ≡ 1 mod their product); the campaign's F_q[T] ES variants (FUNCTIONFIELD_ES*.md) could be fingerprinted on such P.
why: If F_q[T] ES counts at these P are minimal, the 'p ≡ 1 mod smooth' hardness mechanism is structural and transfers to the setting where proofs exist — a template for transferring arguments.
first_step: Using the existing F_q[T] engines (scripts/*ff*), count solutions at P = 1 + T·∏… for q = 3, 5 and compare with random P of the same degree.

title: Function-field analogue of the χ_p Euler-product law
connection: Over F_q[T], fit the ES count at monic irreducible P against Σ_{deg Q ≤ d} χ_P(Q)/|Q| (quadratic character of small-degree irreducibles mod P).
why: If the same law (negative α for 'P ≡ 1 mod 4'-analogue) holds, the count mechanism (Brauer/Hilbert symbol) is characteristic-free and the function-field proofs might reveal how to beat it.
first_step: Pick q = 3, deg P ≤ 10 (≈ 6 000 irreducibles); reuse the F_q[T] solution counters.

title: Pseudosquares over F_q[T] (Lehmer analogue) as the hardest ES inputs
connection: Define F_q[T] pseudosquares (non-square P ≡ square-like mod all small irreducibles); predicted hardest ES inputs if the integer picture transfers.
why: Bridges the integer pseudosquare fingerprint to the setting with proved ES variants.
first_step: Generate F_3[T] pseudosquares up to degree 12 and run the ES solvers.

title: Proof of the isosceles law: x = y ⟺ (4x − 2p)(4z − p) = 2p²
connection: 2/x + 1/z = 4/p ⟺ (4x − 2p)(4z − p) = 2p², so A = 4x − 2p ∈ {2, 2p, 2p²} (≡ 2 mod 4) and B = 4z − p ∈ {p², p, 1} must be ≡ −p (mod 4): impossible iff p ≡ 1 (4). The shape y = z gives (4x − p)(4z − 2p) = 2p² with the same conclusion. Hence isosceles solutions exist ⟺ p ≢ 1 (mod 4) (p odd prime) — confirming the data exactly.
why: A complete, elementary proof of an empirical fingerprint: the degenerate (isosceles) locus of the ES surface is obstructed exactly on the hard class by a mod-4 divisor condition — a miniature T1-type reciprocity obstruction; for general n it predicts failure ⟺ every prime factor of n is ≡ 1 (mod 4) — verified exactly for all 2 ≤ n ≤ 3000 (344 numbers, = A004613 minus 1).
first_step: Write it up as a lemma (the composite case follows from the same factorisation of 2n²); ask whether every certificate line has such a 'degenerate-locus' shadow.

title: Signed sibling 4/n = 1/x + 1/y − 1/z: count fingerprint
connection: For n = 2 it fails (1/x + 1/y − 1/z < 2); for n ≥ 3 check solvability first, then count solutions in a box (z ≤ n²) and fit the same χ_p law. If the signed count follows χ_{−p} or χ_p with opposite sign, the sign structure of ES (SIGN_FIELDS.md) has a data signature.
why: SIGNED_REFACTOR/SIGN_IDENTITY memos propose sign-twisted reformulations; their counts' character dependence tells whether the twist changes the governing field.
first_step: Adapt the counter (y-range unbounded → impose z ≤ n²) and fit at p ≤ 2·10⁴.

title: Sibling 4/n with denominators in an arithmetic progression or geometric constraints
connection: Solutions with y − x = z − y or y² = xz (geometric) are 'rigid' sub-families; their existence sets at primes are new exception sets.
why: Rigid families are where polynomial-identity constructions live; their failure sets indicate which residue classes each rigid family covers.
first_step: Add the two flags to the variant counter and list failures at primes ≤ 10⁵.

title: k-term sibling: 4/p as a sum of 3 unit fractions with all denominators ≤ C·p (bounded height)
connection: The smallest C such that every prime ≤ X has a solution with z ≤ C·p^{a} — with a = 2 every prime ≤ 10⁵ works; find the minimal constant for a = 2 (C = max minz(p)/p²).
why: Effective ES with explicit height is what lattice/geometry-of-numbers approaches would produce; the empirical C is the target.
first_step: Done: max minz(p)/p² = 0.5026 at p = 577 (see the effective-height item); extend to windows at 10⁶, 10⁷.

title: Hard primes vs Wilson / Wolstenholme-type congruences: null test
connection: Wilson quotients (p−1)!+1)/p mod p and Wolstenholme quotients are p-adic invariants of small integers collectively; test correlation with residual U(p).
why: Expected null (ES counts depend on quadratic data); a non-null would be surprising and important.
first_step: Compute Wilson quotient mod p for p ≤ 2·10⁵ (O(p) each — use p ≤ 2·10⁴) and Spearman.

title: ES hardness vs 'p − 1 practical number' (Erdős–Graham denominators)
connection: p − 1 practical (every m ≤ p − 1 a sum of distinct divisors) is common for smooth p − 1; hard primes have smooth p − 1; Egyptian-fraction representability of 1/p-type fractions is classically tied to practical numbers.
why: Links ES hardness to the practical-number literature (Vose, Saias), where Egyptian fraction lengths are controlled by divisor richness.
first_step: Compute 1[p − 1 practical] and its correlation with residual U(p); check whether all 30 hardest primes have p − 1 practical.

title: Erdős–Graham style: least common denominator of ES solutions vs smooth numbers
connection: minlcm(p)/p (least common denominator over solutions, divided by p) — is it always smooth (all prime factors ≤ p^{1/2})? Practical?
why: Egyptian-fraction denominators tend to be smooth; a smoothness law for minlcm would give a search space ('only smooth L need be tried') for certificates.
first_step: Factor minlcm(p)/p for p ≤ 2·10⁵ and record the max of log P⁺/log p.

title: ES solution denominators and the Prouhet–Tarry–Escott / Znám problem: category check
connection: Znám's problem (each n_i divides ∏_{j≠i} n_j + 1) and Egyptian-fraction 'improper' problems share unit-fraction identities; ES solutions with x | yz + 1-type divisibilities could be fingerprinted.
why: Low expectation; recorded as a breadth item because Znám-type divisibility is the 'Sylvester sequence' world where unit-fraction identities are exact.
first_step: Count ES solutions at primes with x | yz ± 1 or y | xz ± 1 and see if any family is universal.

title: U(n) at Sylvester-sequence-related n (2, 3, 7, 43, 1807, …)
connection: Sylvester numbers s_k satisfy 1 = Σ 1/s_i + 1/(s_k − 1); n = 43, 1807 = 13·139: compute U and compare to neighbours.
why: Numbers with built-in unit-fraction identities might have anomalously many ES solutions (an 'easy family' mirror of lcm+1).
first_step: Look up U(43), U(1807) in f4_all_30000.txt; extend to 3263443 = s₅ with the count program.

title: Hard primes and the Ankeny–Artin–Chowla / large fundamental unit regime
connection: Hard primes have large L(1,χ_p) = 2h(p) log ε_p/√p; with h(p) = 1 typically this means a large regulator (long CF period of √p): compute the CF period of √2521, √66529, √193 vs neighbours.
why: Connects ES hardness to Pell-equation size — and to the CF-length formulations (ES₅) via the same continued-fraction machinery.
first_step: Use the classical_feat data: quantile of CF period at the hard primes.

title: Cohen–Lenstra heuristic for h(p) irrelevant; regulator heuristics (Hooley) relevant
connection: Since ES counts follow L(1,χ_p) and h(p) is mostly 1, the distribution of ES counts at p ≡ 1 (4) inherits the distribution of log ε_p/√p (Hooley's conjecture on the average of real quadratic class numbers × regulators).
why: Gives a 'distribution of hardness' prediction: P(U(p) small) ≈ P(L(1,χ_p) large) which is doubly-exponentially small in the size (Granville–Soundararajan distribution of L(1,χ)).
first_step: Compare the empirical tail of residual log U with the Granville–Soundararajan tail for log L(1,χ_p) scaled by α ≈ 0.3.

title: Granville–Soundararajan extreme values: how hard can an ES prime be?
connection: Granville–Soundararajan show L(1,χ_d) reaches ≈ e^γ log log d (up to lower-order terms) for many d; with U ∝ L(1,χ_p)^{−0.3}, the worst primes up to X have U(p) ≳ log³p·(log log p)^{−0.3}… a polylog lower envelope.
why: Heuristic only: if the (unproven, empirically fitted) count law held with lognormal noise, the χ_p mechanism alone would depress counts by at most a (log log)^{O(1)} factor — so ES failures, if any, would have to come from elsewhere; this is a statement about a model, not about ES.
first_step: Formalise as a conditional heuristic: assume U(p) ≈ c log³p L(1,χ_p)^{−α}·(noise); compute P(U(p) = 0) under lognormal noise and sum over p.

title: Siegel-zero scenario check: what if L(1,χ_{−4p}) is tiny?
connection: k₂ and R correlate positively with L(1,χ_{−4p}); an exceptional (Siegel) discriminant −4p would make Type II/(★) starve; Type I is χ_p-driven and unaffected.
why: Suggests ES is robust to Siegel zeros via Type I (complementarity), aligning with the campaign's 'Siegel dichotomy' discussion.
first_step: Look at the primes with the smallest h(−4p)/√p ≤ 2·10⁵ and check that their k₁ is normal.

title: Mordell's six square classes mod 840 are exactly the six ES-hardest classes by count, in the order 1, 121, 361, 169, 529, 289
why: Quantitative refinement of Mordell's theorem: the classes with no polynomial identity are also the classes with the fewest solutions on average, and the ordering inside them (1 hardest, 289 least hard) is a new fingerprint to explain (by 3-, 5-, 7-adic depth: 1 ≡ square of 1 mod everything).
first_step: Explain the order by which of 3, 5, 7 divide p − 1 (class 1: all three; 121 ≡ 1 mod 3,5 and 2 mod 7; 361 ≡ 1 mod 3,8 and 1 mod 5, 4 mod 7; 289 ≡ 4 mod 5, 2 mod 7) and extend to classes mod 9240.

title: n mod 840 explains 64% of the variance of log U(n) (all n ≤ 30 000)
connection: Residual log U(n) (after log n, loglog n) has variance explained 0.16 (n mod 2), 0.24 (mod 4), 0.39 (mod 12), 0.42 (mod 24), 0.43 (mod 30), 0.64 (mod 840); primes q ≥ 11 alone explain ≤ 6%.
why: Most of the ES count's arithmetic fluctuation is a periodic function of n with small period — the 'covering congruence' part; the remaining 36% is where pointwise difficulty lives.
first_step: Compute VE for moduli 840·11, 840·13 and the residual's distribution after removing the mod-9240 mean.

title: Autocorrelation of residual log U(n): lag 840 → 0.60, lag 120 → 0.49, lag 1 → −0.28
connection: The ES count sequence is strongly periodic with period 840 and anti-correlated at lag 1 (consecutive integers have opposite parity / mod-4 behaviour).
why: Ramanujan-expansion structure: U(n) ≈ Σ_q a_q c_q(n) with significant a_q for q | 840 — a clean target for a 'singular series' heuristic for the count over all n (not only primes).
first_step: Fit U(n)/log³n by Ramanujan sums c_q(n), q ≤ 120, and report the top coefficients (are they multiplicative in q?).

title: Ramanujan-sum expansion of the normalised ES count
connection: Compute-and-check: least-squares coefficients a_q in U(n)/log³n ≈ Σ_{q ≤ Q} a_q c_q(n) over n ≤ 30 000.
why: If a_q is (nearly) multiplicative with a_p ≈ −1/p-ish, the count has an Euler-product singular series over n — the all-n analogue of the χ_p law at primes.
first_step: Implement c_q(n) = Σ_{d | gcd(q,n)} μ(q/d) d and fit.

title: No Type I / Type II complementarity: residual corr(k₁, k₂) = +0.70
connection: At p ≡ 1 (4) ≤ 2·10⁵, residual log k₁ and log k₂ correlate +0.70; 250 primes have both below their 5% quantiles vs 22 expected under independence.
why: Kills the hope that 'when Type I is starved Type II is fed' in general — the types share the dominant hardness axis (χ_p, p−1 smoothness); even at lcm(1..19)+1 the split is typical (k₁ = 193, k₂ = 83; an earlier 'Type II overtakes' claim was an overflow artefact).
first_step: Partial correlation of k₁, k₂ after removing the χ_p Euler product: is the residual dependence then ≈ 0 (types independent given local data)?

title: Consecutive primes ≡ 1 (4): residual log U correlation −0.09
connection: Slight negative correlation between neighbouring primes' ES residuals.
why: Likely a residue-class artefact (neighbouring primes in different classes mod 3, 8); a nonzero value after conditioning would indicate a 'short-interval' effect relevant to EXCEPTIONAL_SHORT.md-type arguments.
first_step: Recompute after removing class-mod-840 means.

title: Class ordering within Mordell classes vs 3-adic depth
connection: 1 (mod 840) is hardest, 289 (mod 840) least among the six; p ≡ 1 (mod 9) vs 4,7 (mod 9) inside each class should explain part of it (9 vs 3 depth effect −0.03 measured earlier).
why: Gives the 'next layer' of Mordell's analysis: which further congruence (mod 9, 16, 25, 49, 11, 13) splits each hard class most.
first_step: Within p ≡ 1 (mod 840) primes, compute mean residual by p mod 9·16·25·11·13 factors one at a time.

title: Easiest classes mod 840: 557, 277, 653, 53, 317
connection: These classes have the most ES solutions on average (+0.3 to +0.54 in log); they are non-squares modulo several of 3, 5, 8 at once (e.g. 557 ≡ 2 mod 3, 2 mod 5, 5 mod 8).
why: The easy classes are covered by several identities simultaneously; counting how many Mordell identities cover each class and correlating with the class mean tests 'count ≈ number of covering identities'.
first_step: Enumerate Mordell/ET identity families mod 840 and count multiplicities per class; correlate with class means.

title: Partition function parity p(p) mod 2 vs ES counts (null test)
connection: Brief asks for partition-type comparisons: compute p(n) mod 2 and mod 3 for n ≤ 2·10⁵ (Euler pentagonal recurrence) and correlate with residual U at primes.
why: Expected null (no known link); a positive result would be a genuine surprise linking ES to modular forms of weight −1/2.
first_step: Implement the pentagonal recurrence mod 2/3 in numpy and run the Spearman test.

title: Kloosterman sums K(1,1;p) vs ES counts (null test)
connection: Normalised Kloosterman sums are Sato–Tate distributed; correlate with residual U(p) at p ≤ 2·10⁴.
why: Kloosterman sums appear in the spectral treatment of divisor problems in progressions (the X(n) part); a correlation at the pointwise level would be surprising.
first_step: Compute K(1,1;p) = Σ_x e((x + x⁻¹)/p) for p ≤ 2·10⁴ and Spearman.

title: Type number of quaternion orders vs ES counts
connection: The type number of B_{p,∞} has class-number correction terms (h(−4p), h(−8p), h(−3p)) whose weighting resembles our twist fits; QUATERNION_ES.md relates ES to quaternion orders.
why: If ES counts correlate with the *correction terms* (after removing (p−1)/12 growth), the quaternion picture has a quantitative fingerprint.
first_step: Compute type numbers via Pizer/Eichler formulas for p ≤ 10⁵ and correlate their corrections with residual U, k₂.

title: Supersingular j-invariants in F_p (not F_{p²}): a class-number quantity
connection: ⌊p/12⌋ + ε counts supersingular j over F̄_p (all lie in F_{p²}); the number lying in F_p is a class-number expression (≈ h(−4p)/2 + … for p ≡ 1 (4), involving h(−p), h(−4p)). Correlate it with residual U(p).
why: Ties a modular-curve count to the class-number data that weakly correlate with ES counts (h(−4p): ρ ≈ +0.14 normalised); expected weak.
first_step: Compute #supersingular j ∈ F_p via the class-number formula (or Sage) for p ≤ 10⁵ and Spearman with residual U, k₂.

title: Rank of y² = x³ − p²x / congruent-number curve at p vs ES count
connection: Congruent number curve E_p: y² = x³ − p²x; Tunnell's criterion decides positive rank / congruence (sufficiency conditional on BSD; it does not give the rank); primes p ≡ 5, 7 (8) are congruent (Heegner/Monsky). Compare U(p) by Tunnell class.
why: Tunnell's criterion counts ternary-form representations (x²+2y²+8z² = p) — a theta-series fingerprint; ES may correlate with these ternary counts.
first_step: Compute Tunnell's counts A(p), B(p) for p ≤ 10⁵ and Spearman with residual U(p).

title: Tunnell ternary counts as ES predictors
connection: #{x²+2y²+8z² = p} and #{x²+2y²+32z² = p} are weight-3/2 coefficients; their ratio is Tunnell's congruent-number test. Correlate both with k₁, k₂.
why: A weight-3/2 form whose coefficients track ES counts would be the first concrete 'theta lift' fingerprint (Kudla/Shimura direction).
first_step: Brute-force the representation counts for p ≤ 10⁵ (O(p) each with nested loops ≈ fine for p ≤ 2·10⁴).

title: ES counts vs number of ideal classes of order 2 / genus characters of Q(√−p·m)
connection: Genus theory of Q(√−4p·m) for small m produces characters χ_m·χ_p; our fits show only χ_p-type and χ_{−4p}-type Euler products matter. Test twists by m ∈ {3, 5, 7, 15, 21, 35, 105}.
why: Maps which genus fields 'see' ES hardness; 105 = 3·5·7 appears as a universal small exception elsewhere.
first_step: Fit log U on log L(1, χ_{−mp}) for the listed m jointly.

title: Exceptions are about dispersion, not mean: squarefree-ES (mean 19.8) has 3 exceptions, 20/p (mean 26.4) has 60 still occurring at 9·10⁴
why: Families defined as a 'share' of all solutions (squarefree, lcm-closed, no-3) inherit U's tight distribution and have tiny exception sets; families defined by a multiplicative constraint (k | xyz, the (★) line) have heavy lower tails. For a proof, pick families of the first kind.
first_step: Measure the coefficient of variation of each family's count (residual after log p) and plot last-exception vs CV; test the predicted monotone relation.

title: Share families as proof targets: squarefree / lcm-closed / no-3 sub-ES
connection: Sub-families that are a stable fraction of all solutions (shares 0.15, 0.377, 0.346) have ≤ 3 exceptions ≤ 10⁵, with exceptions among the ES-hardest primes.
why: If a sub-family is a stable share, any lower bound for U(p) transfers with a constant loss only if equidistribution of solutions in the sub-family condition holds pointwise — a precise 'equidistribution' lemma to aim for.
first_step: Test pointwise stability of the share: min over p ∈ [X, 2X] of share(p) vs mean share; if bounded below away from 0, record as conjecture.

title: Exception counting functions per decade stop early
connection: (★) zeros per decade 10²…10¹⁰: 2,2,2,3,5,0,0,0 (last 8 813 281 in a search to 10¹⁰); U failures: last 978145 (to 10⁹); I3: last 2 433 600 (to 3·10⁶ here; campaign to 1e9); Type A: last 66529 (to 10¹¹); 8/p: last 241.
why: Under a dispersion model where P(count = 0) ≈ exp(−c·mean²/var), exceptions die out super-polynomially — consistent with finite exceptional sets for every line; the decade profile is a fit target for c.
first_step: Fit c for (★) using the empirical mean/variance of R(p) at 10⁵–3·10⁶ and predict the expected number of zeros beyond 10⁷ (should be ≪ 1).

title: Sierpiński 5/p hard primes: 8821, 6301, 4201, 12601, 81901, 4621, … all ≡ 1 (mod 20)
connection: Hardest primes for 5/p (residual log U₅) ≤ 10⁵; 4201, 12601, 20521 are also among the hardest for 4/p; residual correlation between U₄ and U₅ is only +0.23.
why: Primes ≡ 1 modulo a smooth number are hard for every numerator (shared 'p − 1 smooth' axis) while the character axes differ by numerator — a decomposition of hardness into universal and numerator-specific parts.
first_step: Fit the Euler-product law for 5/p (per-prime weights) and compare its signs with 4/p.

title: Cross-numerator residual correlations: U₄ vs U₅ 0.23, U₆ 0.50, U₇ 0.16, U₉ 0.26, U₁₃ 0.15
connection: Residual log counts at primes 10³–10⁵ correlate weakly across numerators except 6 (6/p = (4/p)·(3/2) shares structure with 4/p).
why: Different numerators see largely different arithmetic: a joint 'all numerators hard' prime must be p ≡ 1 mod a smooth modulus — 12601 = 2³3²5²7 + 1 is hardest for 4, 5 and 7 simultaneously.
first_step: Cluster primes by their vector of residuals over m = 4..13; identify the universal-hard cluster.

title: 12601 = 12600 + 1: hardest prime across numerators 4, 5, 7
connection: 12601 has U = 27 (rank 26 of 8 966 primes ≡ 1 (4) ≤ 2·10⁵ by U/log³p), is rank 4 for 5/p and rank 1 for 7/p, and fails 15/p; p − 1 = 2³·3²·5²·7.
why: A natural single test case for 'universal' hardness, smaller than 2521-type examples for other numerators.
first_step: List all ES solutions of 4/12601, 5/12601, 7/12601 and identify common structure (denominators' factorisations).

title: Numerator-6 tracks numerator-4 (residual corr 0.50)
connection: 6/p solutions include (3/2)·… rescalings of 4/p-type structures; hardest 6/p primes 1657, 6481, 16561, 21841, 1873, 2521, … overlap 4/p hard lists (21841, 2521, 1873, 20521).
why: 6/p is 'ES with a 2-adic/3-adic twist'; its failure-free status (no 6/p failure ≤ 10⁵) plus shared hardness makes it a natural sibling to prove first.
first_step: Check whether every ES solution family (Type I/II parametrisations) has a 6/p analogue and compare counts.

title: Minimum of U(p)/log³p by decade as the key ES 'safety margin' statistic
why: If m(X) stays bounded below, ES's margin is a constant fraction of the mean — the single number to monitor in any larger census.
first_step: Add U(p)/log³p minima to any future census (count program is ≈ linear in p per prime; windows at 10⁸, 10⁹ feasible).

title: Census design: compute U only at model-predicted hard primes
connection: Since n mod 840 explains 64% and the χ_p Euler product most of the rest, a census of the hardest primes can target ≈ 1% of primes (p ≡ 1, 121, 361, 169, 529, 289 mod 840 with many small QRs).
why: Turns the global lower-envelope question into a feasible computation up to 10¹² for the candidate set.
first_step: Implement the pre-filter (840-class + q ≤ 23 QR count ≥ 6) and run the count on survivors in [10⁹, 10⁹ + 10⁷].

title: Distinct-only count D(p) = U(p) at p ≡ 1 (4); U(p) − D(p) = 2 exactly at every prime p ≡ 3 (4), p > 7
connection: Verified over all primes ≤ 2·10⁵: U − D = 0 at all 8 977 primes ≡ 1 (4) and U − D = 2 at all 9 004 primes ≡ 3 (4) > 7 — the two isosceles solutions predicted by the factorisations (4x−2p)(4z−p) = 2p² and (4x−p)(4z−2p) = 2p².
why: Exact corollary of the proved isosceles law: the distinct and non-distinct ES problems coincide on the hard class, and the orbit-size correction O(p) − 6D(p) is an explicit constant at p ≡ 3 (4).
first_step: Write as a corollary next to the isosceles lemma; the orbit formula O(p) = 6U(p) − 6 (p ≡ 3 mod 4), O(p) = 6U(p) (p ≡ 1 mod 4) holds at every prime 2·10⁴–2·10⁵ (checked); see whether A292624 states it.

title: Independent confirmation of OEIS A400619 (records of 4x(p) − p) up to 2·10⁵
connection: Our engine gives records of 4·(least first denominator) − p at primes 2, 5, 73, 1129, 1201, 21169, 118801 (values 2, 3, 7, 11, 23, 31, 59) — exactly the first seven terms of A400619 (Witteveen 2026, searched to 4·10¹¹; next terms 8 803 369, 119 945 383 009).
why: A400619's primes are the 'greedy-hardest' primes; 21169 is also one of our three all-squarefree failures and 118801, 1201 are top-30 U-hard — the greedy-depth record is a strong hardness detector.
first_step: Compute U, R, Uv at 8 803 369 (≈ 4 s with the count program) — note it is close to but different from the R-zero 8 813 281 — and test whether it is an R-zero or U-hard.

title: OEIS A392469 = records of min k (p | y = kp) over primes p ≡ 1 (mod 24) — reproduced
why: Identifies the entry's implicit restriction (p ≡ 1 mod 24) — a possible clarification for OEIS — and links its comment '(q/p) = 1 for q ≤ 13 for all late terms' to our χ_p Euler-product law.
first_step: Email/edit suggestion for A392469: state the p ≡ 1 (24) restriction or add the all-prime variant; compare k(p) with Cmin(p) of the (★) line.

title: A392469's empirical bound k(p) < 71 log p vs our certificate-size laws
connection: Gold notes k(a(n)) < 71·log a(n) for all known records; our (★) Cmin has mean ≈ 2 with rare large values (23105 at a boundary case), and Vmin ≤ 116 ≤ 3·10⁶.
why: Logarithmic certificate size is exactly what a 'small-certificate covering' approach needs; comparing the k(p) law with the line-specific laws tells which line has the best size profile.
first_step: Plot max_{p ≤ X} k(p)/log p from mink_pr_2e5.txt and compare with Vmin, Cmin records.

title: A139665 (primes x² + 840y²) = Mordell's six hard classes, because 840 is idoneal
connection: Primes of the form x² + 840y² are exactly the primes ≡ 1, 121, 169, 289, 361, 529 (mod 840) (entry comment; Knott links to Mordell 1969); 840 is an Euler idoneal number, so each genus of discriminant −3360 has one class and the principal genus is a congruence condition.
why: Recasts Mordell's obstruction as 'p splits completely in the genus field Q(i, √2, √−3, √5, √−7) of Q(√−210)'; our class ordering (1 ≻ 121 ≻ 361 ≻ 169 ≻ 529 ≻ 289) is then a statement about which ring-class-field data refine hardness; the largest known idoneal number 1848 suggests a mod-1848 analogue.
first_step: Check the 'idoneal' framing: does a Mordell-type covering mod 1848 (or 1320, 1365) leave exactly the principal genus uncovered? Compute which classes mod 1848·5 have polynomial identities.

title: Idoneal numbers as natural covering moduli
connection: Euler's 65 known idoneal numbers (largest 1848; the list is complete under GRH, and at most one more could exist unconditionally — A000926) are exactly the D for which x² + Dy² representing p is a congruence condition; Mordell's modulus 840 is one of them.
why: If ES identities can only cover non-principal genera of some form x² + Dy² (a 'genus obstruction' version of Mordell–Schinzel), the idoneal list would indicate where pure congruence coverings of this kind can reach; for non-idoneal D the principal-form condition is no longer a congruence condition (class-group data).
first_step: For D ∈ {1320, 1365, 1848} compute which classes mod 4D are covered by the known identity families and whether the uncovered set is the principal genus.

title: A287116 (Alekseyev): non-square n not of the form 4M − d with ab | M, d | a+b: only 288, 336, 4545 below 2·10⁹
connection: Dubickas–Novikas' set E(4) formulation; our ESC zero set (no word coordinate in 4ℤ ∪ (8ℤ − n)) contains 288 and 336 too (plus 105, 672, 1380, …), but not 4545.
why: Two different word-type certificate systems share the exceptional values 288 and 336; A287116's finiteness would imply ES (entry comment). Mapping our families onto the 4M − d form unifies the campaign's word families with Dubickas–Novikas.
first_step: Check ESC(4545) and the A287116 condition at 105, 672, 1380; write the explicit dictionary between (t,u,v) words and (M,a,b,d).
refs: Dubickas–Novikas, Acta Math. Univ. Comenianae 81(2), 2012 (as cited by OEIS A287116; https://www.iam.fmph.uniba.sk/amuc/_vol-81/_no_2/_dubickas/dubickas.html — check)

title: A396825/A397366 (van Tol): integers not in the 'S(n)' triangle — 12, 28, 33, 60, 96, 124, 193, 228, 288, 336, 385, …
connection: van Tol's S(n) = {A ≤ 4n−2 : A·X + W ≡ 0 (mod 4n−1) for divisors X, W of n}; complement A396825 contains all squares, all ≡ 0,1,4,9 (mod 12), and includes 193 (a Type-A failure) and 288, 336 (A287116), 12, 28, 60, 96, 124, 228 (our U-zero set Uv = 0).
why: Another divisor-class formulation whose exceptional set overlaps ours: aligning the three (A396825, A287116, our Uv/ESC zero sets) could reveal they are the same obstruction at different normalisations.
first_step: Compute the symmetric differences between A396825 ∩ [1, 3000] and our Uv/ESC/R zero sets; explain 33 and 193.

title: A257843 (Hasler): n where the lexicographically first solution ≠ the max-z solution
why: A 'solution-geometry' fingerprint (shape of the solution set's extremes) — a cheap invariant that may separate hard from easy classes.
first_step: Compute the density of A257843 among p ≡ 1 (24) vs others and correlate membership with residual U(p).

title: A213340 / A213686 / A213687: value sets of the bilinear polynomials 5+8t+12k+16kt etc.
connection: These OEIS entries list the values of ES identity polynomials (Type-like families a + bt + ck + dkt); their union is a covering-by-bilinear-forms description of ES-solvable n.
why: Bilinear value sets are exactly the shape n = tuv − u − v-type words after substitution; their complements in p ≡ 1 (24) should match our hard sets — a direct test of which bilinear families matter.
first_step: Compute the union of the listed bilinear families' values ≤ 10⁶ and compare its complement with the R-, U-, I3-zero sets.

title: OEIS has 2026 ES entries (A392469, A397366, A396825, A400619) — active outside community
connection: Four ES-related sequences were added in 2026 by Gold, van Tol, Witteveen, plus Alekseyev's A287116 (2017); the campaign's hard-prime lists and our variant failure sets are absent.
why: The OEIS ES cluster is an active, low-cost outreach channel; contributing the R-zeros, U failures, I3 zeros, lcm-closed/no-3/squarefree exceptions and the isosceles law would connect to these authors' searches (e.g. Witteveen searched to 4·10¹¹).
first_step: Prepare a batch of 6–8 submissions with b-files and cross-references to A139665, A392469, A400619, A287116.

title: Witteveen's 4·10¹¹ greedy search as a free hardness census
connection: A400619 states no prime in (1.2·10¹¹, 4·10¹¹) reaches 4x − p ≥ 112, i.e. every prime there has a solution with x ≤ (p + 111)/4.
why: A uniform 'small first denominator' statement on the searched range (≤ 4·10¹¹, per A400619) — a bounded-shift ES certificate (shift s = 4x − p ≤ 111) verified far beyond the campaign's U/Vmin censuses; matches our bounded-v observation.
first_step: Ask/derive: does bounded 4x − p (≤ 111) imply a bounded U-certificate v, or vice versa? Compare shift s with Vmin(p) on our data.

title: Greedy depth 4x(p) − p vs Vmin(p): same quantity?
connection: Compute-and-check: both are 'smallest shift' certificates; if 4x(p) − p ≥ Vmin(p) − c always, the U-family bounded-v phenomenon and A400619's bounded-shift phenomenon coincide.
why: Merging two independent small-certificate observations into one would sharpen the empirical 'bounded shift ES' conjecture.
first_step: From mink_pr_2e5.txt (col: min 4x − p) and minwords (Vmin), scatter and report the relation at p ≡ 1 (4).

title: A400619's record prime 8 803 369 is ES-hard (U/log³p = 0.034) but not a (★) zero (R = 16)
connection: U(8803369) = 140 (k₁ = 94, k₂ = 46; overflow-corrected), U/log³p = 0.034 — below the 10⁶/10⁷ window minima 0.044/0.055 and below lcm(1..19)+1 (0.039); words: W = 107, I3 = 68, R = 16, Uv = 11. The nearby R-zero 8 813 281 has W = 127, R = 0.
why: Greedy-depth records are genuinely hard for the full count, while (★) zeros are line-specific: two independent hardness notions pick different primes at the same height.
first_step: Compute the χ_p Euler product and p mod 840 for 8803369 and 8813281; predict which notion each satisfies.

title: Greedy depth 4x(p) − p and U-certificate size Vmin(p) are only weakly related (corr 0.38)
connection: At p ≡ 1 (4) ≤ 2·10⁵: the most common pairs (shift, Vmin) are (3,3), (3,4), (7,4), (7,7); shift ≥ Vmin in 62% of primes; Vmin − shift ranges −27…+113.
why: Two 'bounded small certificate' phenomena (A400619's bounded shift to 4·10¹¹ and our Vmin ≤ 116 to 3·10⁶) are distinct — each gives an independent bounded-certificate conjecture.
first_step: State both conjectures with their empirical bounds and look for a lemma connecting a shift-s solution to a U-certificate with v ≤ f(s).

title: Our ESC zero set ≤ 1369 ⊂ A396825 ∪ {105, 672}
connection: Every n ≤ 1369 with no word having a coordinate in 4ℤ ∪ (8ℤ − n) is in van Tol's A396825 except 105 and 672; Uv zeros differ from A396825 by {33, 193, 385} vs {105, 156, 204, 316, 396, 508, …}.
why: Near-containment between independently defined exception sets suggests a common divisor-class obstruction; making it exact would merge two literatures.
first_step: Fetch the A396825 b-file and test containment to 10⁶; analyse 105 and 672 under van Tol's S(n) definition.

title: 105 = 3·5·7 vs 385 = 5·7·11: products of consecutive odd primes in exceptional sets
connection: 105 is a zero of all our word families; 385 is in A396825 but our families certify it; 33 = 3·11 likewise.
why: Squarefree products of small odd primes are 'locally saturated' (n ≡ 0 mod many small q kills many shifts); a cheap structural family to test any certificate system on: 15015, 255255, …
first_step: Compute R, Uv, I3, ESC at products of consecutive odd primes up to 3·10⁶ (105, 1155, 15015, 255255) and at 3·5·7·m² forms.

title: Σ_{p ≤ N} f(p) / (N log² N) = 0.88, 0.80, 0.77, 0.76, 0.75 (N = 10³…2·10⁵)
connection: ET prove N log²N ≪ Σ_{p≤N} f(p) ≪ N log²N log log N; our ordered counts give a slowly decreasing ratio to N log²N (and 0.45 → 0.30 against N log²N loglog N) — the data favour the lower-bound order, with a constant ≈ 0.7.
why: Suggests (does not pin down) that the log log factor in ET's upper bound may be absent — relevant to which heuristic mean (BM, Euler product) is calibrated correctly.
first_step: Extend to 10⁷ via windows; fit c + d/log N.

title: Σ_{n ≤ N} f(n) grows faster than N log³N in range (ratio 7.6 → 19.6 for N = 10³ → 3·10⁴)
connection: Over all n (composites included) the ordered-count partial sums outgrow N log³N; composite n with many divisors carry large counts.
why: Composite counts are dominated by divisor-rich n; irrelevant to ES existence but important if one uses averages over all n as a proxy for primes (wrong normalisation by a log² factor).
first_step: Check ET's statement for Σ_{n≤N} f(n) (if any) and fit the exponent of log.

title: Targeted count at A400619's 119 945 383 009 (too big for exhaustive count): partial certificates
connection: Count only solutions with x ≤ (p + 200)/4 (shift ≤ 200) and Type II solutions with small y/p at p = 119945383009 using divisor enumeration of p·x — a few minutes.
why: Even a partial count gives a lower bound and its type profile at the hardest known greedy prime; tests whether Type II rescues greedy-hard primes.
first_step: Adapt z52b_fingerprint_count.c with a shift cap and 128-bit arithmetic; run once.

title: Lowest-count composites: are they products of hard primes?
connection: Rank composite n ≤ 30 000 by U(n)/log³n; test whether the lowest are products of two primes both in the hard class (p ≡ 1 mod 24) such as 73·193.
why: If hardness multiplies, composite ES-hardness reduces to prime hardness (expected: composites inherit solutions from each factor, so they should be easy).
first_step: Sort f4_all_30000.txt by U/log³n restricted to composites.

title: ES count vs number of prime factors ≡ 1 (mod 4) of n
connection: For composite n, fit log U(n) on ω₁(n) = #{p | n : p ≡ 1 (4)} and ω₃(n); the isosceles law says ω₃ = 0 kills degenerate solutions for odd n (even n have them anyway); does ω₃ also boost the bulk count?
why: Quantifies how the 'sum of two squares' structure of n influences ES counts beyond the isosceles locus.
first_step: Regress on f4_all_30000.txt.

title: ES counts on the 'norm form' side: n = a² + b² with a/b fixed angle
connection: For n ≡ 1 (4) prime the Gaussian angle was null; for composite n test whether representations as norms from Z[ω], Z[√−2] (x²+3y², x²+2y²) predict counts.
why: Norm-form representability is the genus/class-field data; for primes it reduces to Legendre symbols (already captured), for composites it adds multiplicities.
first_step: Correlate U(n) with r_{x²+y²}(n), r_{x²+2y²}(n), r_{x²+3y²}(n) at composites ≤ 30 000.

title: Distribution of x/p over all solutions (the 'x-profile')
connection: Histogram of x/p ∈ (1/4, 3/4] over all solutions at primes 10⁴–2·10⁵; expect mass near 1/4 (greedy) with a 1/(4x − p)-type law.
why: The x-profile is the density a sieve over x must reproduce; deviations (e.g. secondary peaks at x/p = 1/3, 1/2) show identity families.
first_step: Extend the count program to histogram x/p and y/p.

title: Balanced solutions (z ≤ 10x) frequency
connection: Fraction of primes with a solution having z/x ≤ C for C = 10, 100, 1000; BALANCED_LATTICE.md studies balanced points.
why: If balanced solutions exist for all large p with C fixed, geometry-of-numbers on the cubic surface (bounded-height points) would suffice — a strong statement to falsify cheaply.
first_step: Add a min z/x statistic to the count program and record its maximum over p ≤ 2·10⁵.

title: Ratio y/x and z/y spectra as fingerprints of identity families
connection: Polynomial identity families produce solutions with rational ratios y/x → constants as p grows (e.g. y ≈ 2x); peaks in the empirical distribution of y/x identify which identities fire.
why: A data-driven way to rediscover Mordell-type identities and to see which ones the hard classes lack.
first_step: Histogram log(y/x) over all solutions at p ≤ 2·10⁵ split by class mod 840.

title: Per-class identity 'signatures' mod 840
connection: For each class a mod 840, the set of limiting ratios (y/x, z/x) of solutions common to all primes in the class is its identity signature; hard classes should have empty signatures (no polynomial identity).
why: Makes Mordell–Schinzel's 'no polynomial identity covers square classes' visible in data, and might expose quasi-identities (identities valid for a positive proportion of the class).
first_step: Group solutions by class and ratio buckets; list buckets present for ≥ 90% of primes in the class.

title: Quasi-identities: ratio buckets present for a positive proportion of a hard class
connection: In the six hard classes, find solution families (ratio buckets) present for ≥ 30% of primes; each corresponds to a conditional identity (valid when some auxiliary divisibility holds).
why: Conditional identities with complementary conditions could jointly cover a hard class — a 'covering by conditional identities' strategy whose obstacles the data would show.
first_step: Mine the solution lists of primes ≡ 1 (mod 840) ≤ 2·10⁵ for frequent ratio buckets and their auxiliary conditions.

title: Hard-prime 'twin' structure: p and p + 2520 both hard?
connection: Because hardness depends on p mod 840 and quadratic characters, p and p + 840k share the mod-840 part but not the characters at q ∤ 840; test correlation of residuals at lag 840 among primes.
why: Separates the periodic (mod 840) from the character part: lag-840 correlation among primes estimates their variance shares (cf. 0.60 autocorrelation over all n).
first_step: Compute residual correlation for prime pairs (p, p+840k), k ≤ 10.

title: ES counts for p in Chebotarev classes of the 2-part of the class group of Q(√−p)
connection: For p ≡ 1 (8), the 4-rank of Cl(−4p) is 1 iff p ≡ 1 (8) and 8 | h iff p = x² + 32y² … — null observed for h mod 16; extend to the 2-class field tower data of Q(√−2p), Q(√−6p).
why: Rules out (or finds) dependence of ES on 2-class-group data beyond genus — completing the 'only genus characters matter' fingerprint.
first_step: Compute h(−8p), h(−24p) mod 16 and test as for h(−4p).

title: U(p) and the least prime ≡ 1 (mod p) or the least prime q with p | q − 1 (Linnik-type)
connection: Null-expected cross check: data about primes in progressions modulo p (EXSET_LINNIK.md) should not influence local ES counts.
why: Sanity: separates 'divisor-in-progression' events used in ES (which are about divisors of p-tied integers) from progressions mod p.
first_step: Compute least prime q ≡ 1 (mod p) for p ≤ 2·10⁴ and Spearman with residual U.

title: Hardness vs the order of 10 mod p (decimal period) — category check
connection: Decimal period of 1/p is ord_p(10); a correlation would only reflect (2/p), (5/p) structure already captured.
why: Guards against 'recreational' fingerprints; if a residual correlation remains after controlling for (2/p), (5/p), that is a genuine surprise.
first_step: Partial Spearman of U-residual with ord_p(10)/(p−1) given (2/p), (5/p).

title: Fingerprint of 'ES at p' vs 'ES at 4p+1' / 'ES at (p+3)/4'
connection: The (★) divisor form involves 4Cp + 1 and the greedy step (p+3)/4; test whether U(4p+1) or U((p+3)/4) (when composite, often easy) correlates with U(p).
why: Cheap check of whether ES difficulty propagates along the natural 'p-tied integer' maps (a dynamical view: forests in FOREST_*.md).
first_step: Compute Spearman(U(p), U(4p+1)) for p ≤ 7 500 and Spearman(U(p), U((p+3)/4)).

title: ES count of the Fermat quotient-free / 'ES-easy' family p ≡ −1 (mod 840): exact identities
connection: Record-easy primes are ≡ −1 (mod 840); since p ≡ 3 (4) is trivially ES-solvable, the count excess there measures how many extra identity families fire at −1 modulo 3, 5, 7, 8.
why: The easy-side structure (all identities fire) quantifies the 'maximum covering multiplicity' — the dual of the hard side.
first_step: Mean U(p)/log³p over p ≡ 839 (mod 840) vs other p ≡ 3 (4).

title: Effective height: minz(p) ≤ 0.503·p² for every prime 100 < p ≤ 2·10⁵, extremal at the R-zero 577
connection: max minz(p)/p² = 0.5026 at p = 577 (an R-zero); for p > 1000 the largest log minz/log p is 1.84 (at 6271).
why: An explicit effective-height ES (z ≤ 0.503 p²; minz(577) = 167 330 = 0.50260·577²) holds in range; the extremal prime is again a campaign hard prime, so the height of the cheapest certificate is a hardness detector.
first_step: Track max minz(p)/p² in windows at 10⁶, 10⁷ (count program already outputs minz).

title: Lag-840 correlation at primes: residual log U(p) vs U(p+840) = 0.64 (3 425 pairs); lag 5880: 0.58
connection: Among primes p ≡ 1 (4) with p + 840 also prime, residuals correlate 0.64 — the mod-840 class carries ≈ 60% of the variance at primes too.
why: Confirms at primes what the all-n spectrum showed: ES counts are dominated by a mod-840 periodic component plus a character (q ∤ 840) component.
first_step: Decompose the remaining 40% by p mod 11, 13 and by the χ_p Euler product over q ≥ 11.

title: Hardest composites are prime squares: lowest U(n)/log³n among composites ≤ 30 000 are 97², 113², 163², 109², 37², 67², 2·71², 173², 103², 61², 73², 89²
connection: Eleven of the twelve are prime squares (eight of them squares of primes ≡ 1 (4); 163, 67, 103 are ≡ 3 (4)) and one is 2·71².
why: Count-level shadow of T1: certificate lines vanish at odd squares and the total count at p² is the lowest among composites — squares are the hard composites, as the reciprocity obstruction predicts.
first_step: Compare U(p²) with U(p)² and with the number of solutions inherited from 4/p by scaling.

title: Easy class −1 (mod 840): mean U/log³p = 0.70 vs 0.19 for other p ≡ 3 (4)
connection: Primes p ≡ 839 (mod 840) have 3.6× more ES solutions than other primes ≡ 3 (mod 4) (p > 1000).
why: Quantifies the covering multiplicity at the 'all identities fire' class — the dual extreme to p ≡ 1 (mod 840).
first_step: Count which classical identities apply at p ≡ −1 (mod 840) and check that their solution counts sum to the observed excess.

title: Tunnell's ternary counts: individually weakly correlated with residual U (ρ ≈ 0.18), Tunnell difference A − 2B null (0.02)
connection: For p ≡ 1, 3 (mod 8), 100 < p ≤ 2·10⁴ (1 115 primes): #{x²+2y²+8z² = p} and #{x²+2y²+32z² = p} each correlate +0.19/+0.18 with residual log U(p); A − 2B (congruent-number criterion) ≈ 0.
why: The weight-3/2 theta coefficients share the class-number/genus signal (both ∝ h(−8p)-type quantities) but the congruent-number combination carries nothing: no congruent-number ↔ ES link at the data level.
first_step: Correlate with h(−2p), h(−8p) to confirm the shared signal is just the class number.

title: U(p) vs U((p+3)/4): raw Spearman 0.66; vs U(4p+1): 0.36 (size-confounded)
connection: Raw rank correlations between ES counts at p and at the p-tied integers (p+3)/4 and 4p+1 (p ≤ 30 000 / 7 500).
why: Most of this is the common size trend; the residual correlation (after log n terms on both sides) would show whether difficulty propagates along the greedy map p ↦ (p+3)/4.
first_step: Recompute on residuals; if positive, ES-hardness is 'inherited' along the greedy forest (FOREST_*.md).

title: Hard-prime fingerprints recur across seven distinct (not statistically independent) detectors
connection: 193, 241, 577, 1201, 2521, 3361, 21169 recur among: U/log³ minima, m/p failures (12, 16, 20, 24), greedy-depth records (A400619), min-k records (A392469), height extremes, variant exceptions (lcm-closed, squarefree, no-3, 4|·), R-zeros/Type-A.
why: A small 'hall of fame' of test primes captures most distinct hardness mechanisms; any new idea can be screened in seconds on it.
first_step: Publish the hall of fame with per-detector membership as a table in the campaign (data/z52b/hard_profile.json + variants).

title: Proposed 'hall of fame' test set for ES ideas
why: Breadth lanes generate hundreds of candidate connections; a fixed, diverse hard set makes cheap falsification uniform across lanes.
first_step: Add a script that, given a candidate certificate family (as a predicate on (x,y,z) or words), reports which hall-of-fame primes it certifies.

title: Screening tool: certify-or-not table for any new certificate family
connection: Generalise the variant counter to take a predicate plug-in and output failure sets at primes ≤ 10⁵ in < 1 min (as done for 32 shapes here).
why: Lets other lanes turn 'connection' items into falsifiable data within minutes — the variant runs here found single-exception families (lcm-closed: only 2521) that no theory predicted.
first_step: Refactor scripts/z52b_fingerprint_variants*.c into a predicate-driven engine with a small DSL (divisibility, coprimality, size).

title: Isosceles law generalised to m/p: when do solutions with two equal denominators exist?
connection: For m/p = 2/x + 1/z: (mx − 2p)(mz − p) = 2p²; existence ⟺ a factor pair of 2p² in classes mod m — e.g. m = 5: classes of p mod 5 and 10 decide.
why: Gives exact degenerate-locus laws for every numerator, a family of provable statements mirroring the hard classes for each m.
first_step: Work out m = 5, 7, 8 explicitly and verify with the variant counter.

title: Degenerate-locus obstruction as a model for T1
connection: The isosceles locus of 4/p is obstructed exactly on p ≡ 1 (4) by a mod-4 factor-class argument on 2p²; T1 (all certificate lines empty at odd squares) is a reciprocity obstruction on p-tied integers.
why: Both are 'a fixed integer built from p has no divisor in a required class' — the isosceles case is the 0-dimensional toy model of the line obstructions, fully understood; studying how the obstruction disappears when one moves off the degenerate locus could illuminate why lines fail only at squares.
first_step: Parametrise near-isosceles solutions (y − x small) and compute when their divisor-class condition becomes solvable for p ≡ 1 (4).

title: Near-isosceles solutions: smallest y − x (or z − y) at p ≡ 1 (4)
connection: Since x = y is impossible at p ≡ 1 (4), the minimal gap y − x over solutions is a fingerprint of how close the hard class comes to the degenerate locus.
why: If the minimal gap is always small (bounded or ≪ log p), near-degenerate families might give uniform certificates.
first_step: Add min(y − x) and min(z − y) to the count program; tabulate at p ≡ 1 (4) ≤ 2·10⁵.
